Variance Reduction for Expectations with Diffusion Teachers

Jesse Bettencourt Affiliation: University of Toronto    Xindi Wu Affiliation: Princeton UniversityProject page: research.nvidia.com/labs/sil/projects/CARV/    Matan Atzmon Affiliation: NVIDIA    James Lucas Affiliation: NVIDIA    Jonathan Lorraine Affiliation: NVIDIA
Abstract

Pretrained diffusion models serve as frozen teachers feeding downstream pipelines such as text-to-3D, single-step distillation, and data attribution. The teacher gradients these pipelines consume are Monte Carlo (MC) expectations over noise levels and Gaussian noise samples; their estimator variance dominates compute cost because each draw requires expensive upstream work (rendering, simulation, encoding). We introduce CARV, a compute-aware variance-accounting framework that motivates a hierarchical MC estimator: amortize the expensive upstream computation over cheap diffusion-noise resamples, sharpened by timestep importance sampling and a stratified-inverse-CDF construction. In our text-to-3D distillation and attribution experiments, CARV delivers 22-3×3\times effective compute multipliers (most from amortized reuse; ∼25%{\sim}25\% additional from IS+stratification) without changing the objective; in single-step distillation, the same techniques cut gradient variance by an order of magnitude but do not improve downstream FID, marking the regime where MC variance is no longer the bottleneck.

1 Introduction

Diffusion models underlie leading systems for images, video, audio, and 3D/4D. They also serve as frozen “teachers” supplying gradients to downstream pipelines: text-guided 3D, one-step generator training, and gradient-based attribution. These teacher gradients are Monte Carlo expectations over noise levels and Gaussian noise; each draw requires expensive upstream work (rendering, simulation, encoding), so estimator variance dominates the compute cost. At the lab scale, this is a six- to seven-figure budget. We show simple unbiased techniques that match the same variance at ∼1/3−1/2\sim\!\nicefrac{{1}}{{3}}\!-\!\nicefrac{{1}}{{2}} the cost (22-3×3\times effective compute multipliers).

Most variance-reduction work targets teacher training via loss reweighting and schedule design. Downstream, practitioners inherit teacher timestep distributions, apply ad hoc averaging, introduce bias, and tune compute without a principled view of which sources of randomness dominate and how cost factors in. This leaves three open questions: which estimator components dominate variance, how to reduce variance without biasing the objective, and how to trade cheap operations (noising, denoising) against expensive ones (rendering, encoding) under a fixed budget.

We propose CARV, a compute-aware variance-accounting view of frozen-teacher gradients, motivating practical estimator design choices. The resulting drop-ins are unbiased under the stated sampling construction and improve variance per unit compute in our text-to-3D distillation and attribution settings, with no downstream FID gain in single-step distillation. Our contributions include:

  1. 1.

    Hierarchical Monte Carlo estimator via amortized resampling. Cache expensive upstream computation (renderer/encoder/generator forward passes) and resample cheap diffusion noise (Fig. 3); the dominant lever for our effective compute multiplier (ECM, Sec. 3.2).

  2. 2.

    Timestep importance sampling using the explicit teacher weight. A drop-in proposal q∝p​wq\!\propto\!p\,w giving ∼1.2×{\sim}1.2\times variance reduction over uniform at equal per-iteration cost (Table 2; toy in Fig. 1).

  3. 3.

    Stratified-inverse-CDF sampling over noise levels. Combines stratification with importance sampling (Fig. 2, Fig. 4); near-optimal among unbiased allocations (App. Sec. D.1.6).

  4. 4.

    Compute-aware variance-accounting framework (CARV) with broad evaluation. A measurement framework for diffusion gradient variance (Sec. 3.2, Fig. 5) applied to diffusion-teacher-guided optimization (Sec. 4.1), one-step distillation (Sec. 4.2), and data attribution (Sec. 4.3).

2 Background

We cover diffusion models in Sec. 2.1, variance reduction methods in Sec. 2.2, and variance-bounded diffusion applications in Sec. 2.3 with more details in App. Sec. B.

2.1 Diffusion Models

We use conditional latent diffusion via an autoencoder [16, 64]. Let (𝐱,𝐜)(\mathbf{x},\mathbf{c}) be a data point and its conditioning (e.g., image+text), and 𝐳=Encode​(𝐱)\mathbf{z}\!=\!\textnormal{Encode}(\mathbf{x}) its latent code. Forward noising at level t:→1t\!:\!0\!\to\!1 makes 𝐳t=αt​𝐳+σt​ϵ\mathbf{z}_{t}=\alpha_{t}\mathbf{z}+\sigma_{t}\boldsymbol{\epsilon} with ϵ∼𝒩⁡(𝟎,𝐈)\boldsymbol{\epsilon}\sim\mathcal{N}(\mathbf{0},\mathbf{I}), where αt,σt\alpha_{t},\sigma_{t} are schedule-dependent coefficients (clamped away from t=0t\!=\!0). We use continuous notation; many systems use a discrete grid of TT timesteps.

Weighted diffusion training objective. Let ϵ^ϕ​(𝐳t,t,𝐜)\hat{\boldsymbol{\epsilon}}_{{\boldsymbol{\phi}}}(\mathbf{z}_{t},t,\mathbf{c}) be the predicted noise at (𝐳t,t,𝐜)(\mathbf{z}_{t},t,\mathbf{c}) with parameters ϕ{\boldsymbol{\phi}}. A common noise-prediction objective is:

ℒDiff​(ϕ)=𝔼(𝐱,𝐜),t,ϵ[‖𝐫‖22]=𝔼(𝐱,𝐜),t,ϵ[ℓDiff​(Encode​(𝐱),𝐜,t,ϵ,ϕ)]\smash{\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{Diff}}({\boldsymbol{\phi}})\!=\!\Eop_{(\mathbf{x},\mathbf{c}),t,\boldsymbol{\epsilon}}\!\big[\|\mathbf{r}\|_{2}^{2}\big]\!=\!\Eop_{(\mathbf{x},\mathbf{c}),t,\boldsymbol{\epsilon}}\!\big[\ell_{\mathrm{Diff}}(\textnormal{Encode}(\mathbf{x}),\mathbf{c},t,\boldsymbol{\epsilon},{\boldsymbol{\phi}})\big]} (1)

where the residual 𝐫:=ϵ^ϕ​(𝐳t,t,𝐜)−ϵ\mathbf{r}:=\hat{\boldsymbol{\epsilon}}_{{\boldsymbol{\phi}}}(\mathbf{z}_{t},t,\mathbf{c})-\boldsymbol{\epsilon} and the per-sample cost ℓDiff:=‖𝐫‖22\ell_{\mathrm{Diff}}:=\|\mathbf{r}\|^{2}_{2}. Following Kingma et al. [25], we use the weighted objective:

ℒwDiff​(ϕ)=𝔼(𝐱,𝐜),t,ϵ[w⁡(t)​ℓDiff​(Encode​(𝐱),𝐜,t,ϵ,ϕ)].\!\!\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{wDiff}}({\boldsymbol{\phi}})\!=\!\!\!\Eop_{(\mathbf{x},\mathbf{c}),t,\boldsymbol{\epsilon}}\!\!\big[\!w(t)\ell_{\mathrm{Diff}}(\textnormal{Encode}(\mathbf{x}),\mathbf{c},t,\boldsymbol{\epsilon},{\boldsymbol{\phi}})\!\big].\vskip-1.65329pt (2)

Different prediction parameterizations (e.g., xx- or vv-prediction) can be written in this form with an appropriate choice of w⁡(t)w(t) and the corresponding model output [25]. App. Sec. B.1.1 covers the essentials of sampling from diffusion models and classifier-free guidance. Sec. 2.2.1 covers diffusion noise schedules and their connection to importance sampling.

2.2 Reducing Estimator Variance

We consider Monte Carlo estimators for expectations that arise in diffusion training and downstream uses of frozen diffusion teachers. These are typically vector-valued (e.g., a parameter gradient or an update direction), so for an unbiased estimator 𝝁^\hat{\boldsymbol{\mu}} of a vector mean 𝝁\boldsymbol{\mu}, mean-squared error and variance coincide, and we measure dispersion by:

Var⁡(𝝁^):=𝔼⁡[‖𝝁^−𝝁‖22]=tr⁡(Cov⁡(𝝁^)).\mathrm{Var}(\hat{\boldsymbol{\mu}}):=\mathbb{E}[\|\hat{\boldsymbol{\mu}}-\boldsymbol{\mu}\|_{2}^{2}]=\mathrm{tr}(\mathrm{Cov}(\hat{\boldsymbol{\mu}})). (3)

2.2.1 Importance Sampling & Noise Schedules

Importance sampling reduces Monte Carlo variance by sampling from important regions while keeping the expectation via a likelihood ratio. For noise level t∈[0,1]t\!\in\![0,1] with base density p⁡(t)p(t) and randomness 𝝃\boldsymbol{\xi}, we estimate the mean:

𝝁=𝔼t∼p,𝝃∼p(⋅∣t)[𝐟(t,𝝃)]\smash{\boldsymbol{\mu}=\mathbb{E}_{t\sim p,\boldsymbol{\xi}\sim p(\cdot\mid t)}[\mathbf{f}(t,\boldsymbol{\xi})]} (4)

where 𝐟⁡(t,𝝃)\mathbf{f}(t,\boldsymbol{\xi}) is a vector-valued contribution such as a gradient. Sampling t(n)∼qt^{(n)}\sim q with importance weight w~​(t)=p​(t)/q​(t)\tilde{w}(t)=p(t)/q(t) gives the unbiased estimator:

𝝁^q=1/N​∑n=1Nw~​(t(n))​𝐟​(t(n),𝝃(n)).\hat{\boldsymbol{\mu}}_{q}=\nicefrac{{1}}{{N}}\sum\nolimits_{n=1}^{N}\tilde{w}(t^{(n)})\mathbf{f}(t^{(n)},\boldsymbol{\xi}^{(n)}). (5)

The variance-minimizing proposal is q⋆​(t)∝p⁡(t)​𝔼⁡[‖𝐟⁡(t,𝝃)‖22∣t]q^{\star}(t)\!\propto\!p(t)\sqrt{\mathbb{E}[\|\mathbf{f}(t,\boldsymbol{\xi})\|_{2}^{2}\mid t]} [65]. This oracle is impractical, so practitioners use cheap surrogates such as the per-timestep loss [52, 98] or learned schedules [25]. The right surrogate depends on the form of 𝐟\mathbf{f}, which is task-specific; we instantiate q⋆q^{\star} and pick a proxy for the SDS gradient in Sec. 3.1.2. As shown in Fig. 1 (left), the oracle proposal is variance-equivalent to ∼−4×\sim\!3\!-\!4\times uniform compute and a Gaussian-at-peak approximation to ∼2×\sim\!2\times; full derivation in App. Sec. B.2.

Noise Schedules as Importance Sampling: A noise schedule defines how signal and noise coefficients αt,σt\alpha_{t},\sigma_{t} vary with t∈[0,1]t\in[0,1]. With uniform sampling t∼𝒰⁡(0,1)t\sim\mathcal{U}(0,1), a schedule induces a distribution over noise levels. Schedule design can thus be viewed as choosing an importance distribution for the diffusion training objective; Kingma et al. [25] parametrizes this in terms of signal-to-noise ratio and learns a schedule that minimizes the variance of the training-objective estimator. In downstream tasks, the schedule is inherited from the pretrained teacher, so we augment the timestep distribution via explicit importance sampling (Sec. 3.1.2) rather than retraining. See App. Sec. B.2.2 for details.

2.2.2 Stratified Sampling

Stratified sampling – visualized in Fig. 2 – reduces variance by partitioning the domain into BB disjoint strata and averaging estimates within strata before combining with probabilities. Partition the domain into strata {𝒮b}b=1B\{\mathcal{S}_{b}\}_{b=1}^{B} with probabilities pbp_{b} and MbM_{b} samples per stratum. The estimator is:

𝝁^strat=∑b=1Bpb​1Mb​∑m=1Mb𝐅⁡(tb,m),tb,m∼p⁡(t∣𝒮b)\!\!\hat{\boldsymbol{\mu}}_{\mathrm{strat}}\!\!=\!\!\sum\nolimits_{b=1}^{B}\!p_{b}\!\frac{1}{M_{b}}\!\!\sum\nolimits_{m=1}^{M_{b}}\!\!\mathbf{F}(t_{b,m}),\,t_{b,m}\!\!\sim p(t\!\mid\!\mathcal{S}_{b})\vskip-1.65329pt (6)

This estimator is unbiased for 𝔼t∼p⁡(t)​[𝐅​(t)]\mathbb{E}_{t\sim p(t)}[\mathbf{F}(t)] and has variance no greater than standard IID sampling from p⁡(t)p(t), with strict reduction whenever 𝐅⁡(t)\mathbf{F}(t) varies within the support of p⁡(t)p(t) [80]. As a simple example with a continuous domain t∈[0,1]t\in[0,1], one can use BB equal-width bins. When batch size equals BB with Mb=1M_{b}=1, each bin contributes exactly one draw. We later apply this to diffusion-model estimators by stratifying timestep tt; see Sec. 3.1.3.

2.3 Diffusion Model Applications

2.3.1 Diffusion Priors for Optimization

Score Distillation Sampling (SDS) uses a frozen pretrained diffusion model to supply gradients to a differentiable generator, renderer, or simulator, and underlies text-guided 3D/4D, material, and audio optimization [58, 2, 33, 10, 63]. Given generator parameters 𝜽{\boldsymbol{\theta}} and rendering condition 𝐪\mathbf{q} (e.g., camera pose), we form an encoded observation:

𝐳=g⁡(𝜽,𝐪)=Encode​(g′​(𝜽,𝐪))\smash{\mathbf{z}=g({\boldsymbol{\theta}},\mathbf{q})=\textnormal{Encode}(g^{\prime}({\boldsymbol{\theta}},\mathbf{q}))} (7)

and use the teacher to update 𝜽{\boldsymbol{\theta}}. With 𝐳t=αt​𝐳+σt​ϵ\mathbf{z}_{t}=\alpha_{t}\mathbf{z}+\sigma_{t}\boldsymbol{\epsilon} and residual 𝐫=ϵ^ϕ​(𝐳t,t,𝐜,ω)−ϵ\mathbf{r}=\hat{\boldsymbol{\epsilon}}_{{\boldsymbol{\phi}}}(\mathbf{z}_{t},t,\mathbf{c};\omega)-\boldsymbol{\epsilon}, SDS uses proxy score-direction w⁡(t)​𝐫​d​𝐳t/d​𝐳w(t)\mathbf{r}\,\mathrm{d}\mathbf{z}_{t}/\mathrm{d}\mathbf{z} and applies the chain rule:

𝐮SDS​(𝜽)=𝔼𝐪,t,ϵ[wSDS​(t)​𝐫​d​𝐳/d​𝜽],where ​wSDS​(t)=w⁡(t)​αt​ (using ​d​𝐳t/d​𝐳=αt​𝐈​)\smash{\mathbf{u}_{\textnormal{SDS}}({\boldsymbol{\theta}})\!=\!\Eop_{\mathbf{q},t,\boldsymbol{\epsilon}}\!\big[w_{\textnormal{SDS}}(t)\,\mathbf{r}\,\nicefrac{{\mathrm{d}\mathbf{z}}}{{\mathrm{d}{\boldsymbol{\theta}}}}\big],\ \text{where }w_{\textnormal{SDS}}(t)\!=\!w(t)\alpha_{t}\text{ (using }\nicefrac{{\mathrm{d}\mathbf{z}_{t}}}{{\mathrm{d}\mathbf{z}}}\!=\!\alpha_{t}\mathbf{I}\text{)}} (8)

so wSDS​(t)w_{\textnormal{SDS}}(t) absorbs schedule factors, simplifying backprop and enabling importance sampling. The teacher is frozen; stop-gradient surrogate in App. Sec. B.3.1.

2.3.2 Single-Step Diffusion Distillation

Distribution Matching Distillation (DMD) [94] distills a multi-step teacher into a one-step generator G𝜽G_{{\boldsymbol{\theta}}} that maps Gaussian noise to samples. Minimizing the reverse KL between generator distribution pfakep_{\mathrm{fake}} and data distribution prealp_{\mathrm{real}} yields a gradient as the score difference 𝐬real​(𝐳)=∇𝐳​log​preal​(𝐳)\smash{\mathbf{s}_{\mathrm{real}}(\mathbf{z})=\nabla_{\mathbf{z}}\log p_{\mathrm{real}}(\mathbf{z})} minus 𝐬fake​(𝐳)=∇𝐳​log​pfake​(𝐳)\smash{\mathbf{s}_{\mathrm{fake}}(\mathbf{z})=\nabla_{\mathbf{z}}\log p_{\mathrm{fake}}(\mathbf{z})}:

∇𝜽DKL=𝔼𝐳∼pfake​[(𝐬fake​(𝐳)−𝐬real​(𝐳))​∂G𝜽​(ϵ)∂𝜽].\nabla_{\boldsymbol{\theta}}D_{\mathrm{KL}}=\mathbb{E}_{\mathbf{z}\sim p_{\mathrm{fake}}}[(\mathbf{s}_{\mathrm{fake}}(\mathbf{z})-\mathbf{s}_{\mathrm{real}}(\mathbf{z}))\tfrac{\partial G_{{\boldsymbol{\theta}}}(\boldsymbol{\epsilon})}{\partial{\boldsymbol{\theta}}}]. (9)

DMD computes this gradient by perturbing samples with noise at multiple timesteps tt and approximating scores on noised samples 𝐳t=αt​𝐳+σt​ϵ\mathbf{z}_{t}=\alpha_{t}\mathbf{z}+\sigma_{t}\boldsymbol{\epsilon}. The real score uses the pretrained teacher 𝝁base\boldsymbol{\mu}_{\mathrm{base}}, whereas the fake score uses a learned model 𝝁fakeϕ\boldsymbol{\mu}_{\mathrm{fake}}^{{\boldsymbol{\phi}}} that tracks the generator distribution. This yields a Monte Carlo gradient estimator:

∇𝜽DKL≃𝔼ϵ,t,ϵ′[w⁡(t)​αt​(𝐬fake​(𝐳t,t)−𝐬real​(𝐳t,t))​∂G𝜽​(ϵ)∂𝜽]\!\!\!\nabla_{\!{\boldsymbol{\theta}}}\!D_{\mathrm{KL}}\!\simeq\!\!\!\Eop_{\boldsymbol{\epsilon},t,\boldsymbol{\epsilon}^{\prime}}\!\!\left[\!w(t)\alpha_{t}\!(\mathbf{s}_{\mathrm{fake}}\!(\mathbf{z}_{t},\!t)\!-\!\mathbf{s}_{\mathrm{real}}\!(\mathbf{z}_{t},\!t)\!)\tfrac{\partial G_{{\boldsymbol{\theta}}}(\boldsymbol{\epsilon})}{\partial{\boldsymbol{\theta}}}\!\right]\vskip-2.75269pt (10)

where w⁡(t)w(t) stabilizes and the expectation is over generator input noise ϵ\boldsymbol{\epsilon}, timesteps tt, and forward noise ϵ′\boldsymbol{\epsilon}^{\prime} forming 𝐳t\mathbf{z}_{t}. The fake model 𝝁fakeϕ\boldsymbol{\mu}_{\mathrm{fake}}^{{\boldsymbol{\phi}}} uses an auxiliary denoising loss on stop-gradient outputs, and an optional regression loss aligns the generator with teacher samples on a paired set.

Like Sec. 2.3.1, this gradient is a Monte Carlo expectation over timesteps and noise, so we apply our variance-reduction framework. Details in App. Sec. B.3.2.

2.3.3 Data Attribution for Video Generation

Data attribution quantifies how training examples contribute to a model’s outputs. In generative modeling, this identifies influential/harmful fine-tuning clips for targeted data selection, debugging, and efficient specialization. Classical influence functions measure test loss change from infinitesimal upweighting of a training example, requiring inverse-Hessian-vector products infeasible at scale [26]. Practical alternatives approximate influence via gradient similarity (e.g., TracIn and TRAK) [59, 55]. For diffusion/flow-matching teachers, training losses and gradients are expectations over noise levels and Gaussian noise. A typical attribution score averages cosine similarity of normalized per-example gradients over shared (t,ϵ)(t,\boldsymbol{\epsilon}) draws [91]:

I⁡(query,n)=1|𝒯|​∑(t,ϵ)∈𝒯𝐠query​(t,ϵ)‖𝐠query​(t,ϵ)‖2⊤​𝐠n​(t,ϵ)‖𝐠n​(t,ϵ)‖2\!\!\!I(\mathrm{query},n)\!=\!\frac{1}{|\mathcal{T}|}\!\!\sum_{(t,\boldsymbol{\epsilon})\in\mathcal{T}}\!\!\frac{\mathbf{g}_{\mathrm{query}}(t,\boldsymbol{\epsilon})}{\|\mathbf{g}_{\mathrm{query}}(t,\boldsymbol{\epsilon})\|_{2}}^{\!\!\top}\!\!\frac{\mathbf{g}_{n}(t,\boldsymbol{\epsilon})}{\|\mathbf{g}_{n}(t,\boldsymbol{\epsilon})\|_{2}} (11)

where 𝐠\mathbf{g} is the per-example gradient ∇ϕℓDiff\nabla_{{\boldsymbol{\phi}}}\ell_{\mathrm{Diff}} and subscripts index training and query examples. Sharing (t,ϵ)(t,\boldsymbol{\epsilon}) reduces ranking variance, while per-draw normalization mitigates scale effects. This estimator has substantial Monte Carlo variance, making stable influence rankings expensive.

For video data attribution, MOTIVE [87] further reweights the attribution loss toward dynamic regions using motion masks, corrects for video-length scaling effects, and efficiently projects gradients for scalability. In our experiments (Sec. 4.3), we adopt this motion-centric setup and focus on variance reduction for the underlying (t,ϵ)(t,\boldsymbol{\epsilon}) estimator used to compute influence scores. Further background details are in App. Sec. B.3.3.

3 Our Method

We present CARV: three simple variance-reduction strategies (Sec. 3.1), assessed with a compute-aware variance-estimation framework (Sec. 3.2), and applied to diffusion tasks (Sec. 4); details in App. Sec. C.

3.1 Simple and Cheap Variance Reduction

We investigate three standard, inexpensive strategies: reusing intermediate compute (Sec. 3.1.1), importance sampling (Sec. 3.1.2), and stratified sampling (Sec. 3.1.3).

3.1.1 Variance Reduction via Compute Reuse

Motivation. Diffusion gradient estimators have two types of randomness: expensive upstream operations (rendering in SDS, or generator forward passes in distillation) and cheap noise variables (timesteps tt and Gaussian noise ϵ\boldsymbol{\epsilon}). The naïve approach resamples both per gradient sample. Instead, we cache each expensive operation and re-noise it multiple times with fresh (t,ϵ)(t,\boldsymbol{\epsilon}) draws. Since denoising is much cheaper than rendering or generation, this trades small per-sample cost for many more effective samples, reducing variance per unit compute. See Fig. 3.

Standard one-shot estimator. Let 𝐟⁡(𝐱,t,ϵ)\mathbf{f}(\mathbf{x},t,\boldsymbol{\epsilon}) denote the vector multiplying the renderer Jacobian in the gradient. For SDS (Sec. 2.3.1) with residual 𝐫=ϵ^ϕ​(𝐳t,t,𝐜)−ϵ\smash{\mathbf{r}=\hat{\boldsymbol{\epsilon}}_{{\boldsymbol{\phi}}}(\mathbf{z}_{t},t,\mathbf{c})-\boldsymbol{\epsilon}}, we have 𝐟⁡(𝐱,t,ϵ)=wSDS​(t)​𝐫\smash{\mathbf{f}(\mathbf{x},t,\boldsymbol{\epsilon})=w_{\textnormal{SDS}}(t)\mathbf{r}}. An analogous term appears in the DMD generator gradient (Sec. 2.3.2). The standard estimator uses a fresh render 𝐱(r)=g⁡(𝜽,𝐪(r))\smash{\mathbf{x}^{(r)}=g({\boldsymbol{\theta}},\mathbf{q}^{(r)})} per sample:

∇^𝜽naive=1/R​∑r=1R𝐟⁡(𝐱(r),t(r),ϵ(r))​∂𝐱(r)/∂𝜽\smash{\hat{\nabla}_{{\boldsymbol{\theta}}}^{\mathrm{naive}}=\nicefrac{{1}}{{R}}\sum\nolimits_{r=1}^{R}\mathbf{f}(\mathbf{x}^{(r)},t^{(r)},\boldsymbol{\epsilon}^{(r)})\nicefrac{{\partial\mathbf{x}^{(r)}}}{{\partial{\boldsymbol{\theta}}}}} (12)

where (𝐪(r),t(r),ϵ(r))(\mathbf{q}^{(r)},t^{(r)},\boldsymbol{\epsilon}^{(r)}) are IID, with cost R⁡(crender+encode+cdenoise)R(c_{\mathrm{render+encode}}+c_{\mathrm{denoise}}) and crender+encodec_{\mathrm{render+encode}} including forward/backward through rendering and encoding.

Amortized re-noising of cached states. Generate RR independent renders (e.g., different camera poses in SDS, or different noise inputs in DMD) and for each draw KK pairs (t,ϵ)(t,\boldsymbol{\epsilon}). For SDS, sample 𝐪(r)\mathbf{q}^{(r)} and compute 𝐱(r)=g⁡(𝜽,𝐪(r))\mathbf{x}^{(r)}=g({\boldsymbol{\theta}},\mathbf{q}^{(r)}) for r=1,…,Rr=1,\dots,R. The re-use estimator is:

∇^𝜽reuse=1R​∑r=1R(1K​∑k=1K𝐟⁡(𝐱(r),t(r,k),ϵ(r,k)))​∂𝐱(r)∂𝜽\!\hat{\nabla}_{{\boldsymbol{\theta}}}^{\mathrm{reuse}}\!=\!\frac{1}{R}\!\sum\nolimits_{r=1}^{R}\!\Big(\frac{1}{K}\!\!\sum\nolimits_{k=1}^{K}\!\mathbf{f}(\mathbf{x}^{\!(r)}\!\!,t^{\!(r,k)}\!\!,\boldsymbol{\epsilon}^{\!(r,k)})\!\Big)\!\frac{\partial\mathbf{x}^{\!(r)}}{\partial{\boldsymbol{\theta}}} (13)

This is unbiased because (t,ϵ)(t,\boldsymbol{\epsilon}) resample independently of 𝐱(r)\mathbf{x}^{(r)}, at cost ≈R⁡(crender+encode+K​cdenoise)\smash{\approx R(c_{\mathrm{render+encode}}+Kc_{\mathrm{denoise}})}. For a fixed budget, take KK large whenever crender+encode≫cdenoisec_{\mathrm{render+encode}}\gg c_{\mathrm{denoise}}, which often holds because crender+encodec_{\mathrm{render+encode}} includes backprop through the renderer or generator while cdenoisec_{\mathrm{denoise}} uses only the frozen teacher. With latent diffusion, compute 𝐳(r)=Encode​(𝐱(r))\mathbf{z}^{(r)}=\textnormal{Encode}(\mathbf{x}^{(r)}) once per render and form 𝐳t(r,k)=αt​𝐳(r)+σt​ϵ(r,k)\mathbf{z}_{t}^{(r,k)}=\alpha_{t}\mathbf{z}^{(r)}+\sigma_{t}\boldsymbol{\epsilon}^{(r,k)} for all kk, removing repeated encoder cost while keeping Eq. 13 unbiased.

Re-noising can also help when crender+encode≤cdenoisec_{\mathrm{render+encode}}\leq c_{\mathrm{denoise}}. By the law of total variance, estimator variance decomposes into across-render variability (1/R1/R) and within-render conditional variance from (t,ϵ)(t,\boldsymbol{\epsilon}) (1/(R⋅K)1/(R\cdot K)). Re-noising reduces the latter at low marginal cost.

Concretely. SDS. Per step, sample RR poses 𝐪(r)\mathbf{q}^{(r)}, render 𝐱(r)=g⁡(𝜽,𝐪(r))\mathbf{x}^{(r)}=g({\boldsymbol{\theta}},\mathbf{q}^{(r)}) once each, and (for latent diffusion) encode 𝐳(r)\mathbf{z}^{(r)} once; for each rr draw KK pairs (t,ϵ)(t,\boldsymbol{\epsilon}) and backpropagate once per render via Eq. 13. One-step distillation. Treat the generator output 𝐳(r)=G𝜽​(ϵ(r))\mathbf{z}^{(r)}=G_{{\boldsymbol{\theta}}}(\boldsymbol{\epsilon}^{(r)}) as the expensive state and apply the same re-noising pattern with fresh (t,ϵ′)(t,\boldsymbol{\epsilon}^{\prime}). Combined pseudocode in Algorithm 1.

3.1.2 Importance Sampling Strategies

From Sec. 3.1.1, the SDS per-sample contribution multiplying the renderer Jacobian is 𝐟⁡(𝐱,t,ϵ)=wSDS​(t)​𝐫\mathbf{f}(\mathbf{x},t,\boldsymbol{\epsilon})\!=\!w_{\textnormal{SDS}}(t)\,\mathbf{r}, giving parameter-gradient form wSDS​(t)​𝐉𝜽⊤​𝐫w_{\textnormal{SDS}}(t)\,\mathbf{J}_{{\boldsymbol{\theta}}}^{\top}\mathbf{r} at fixed render. The variance-minimizing proposal from Sec. 2.2.1 is then q⋆​(t)∝p⁡(t)​𝔼⁡[‖wSDS​𝐉𝜽⊤​𝐫‖22∣t]q^{\star}(t)\!\propto\!p(t)\sqrt{\mathbb{E}[\|w_{\textnormal{SDS}}\mathbf{J}_{{\boldsymbol{\theta}}}^{\top}\mathbf{r}\|_{2}^{2}\!\mid\!t]}, which requires per-timestep gradient norms over renders and noise and is impractical. Loss-based proxies use only ‖𝐫‖22\|\mathbf{r}\|_{2}^{2} and ignore wSDS2w_{\textnormal{SDS}}^{2} and ‖𝐉𝜽‖22\|\mathbf{J}_{{\boldsymbol{\theta}}}\|_{2}^{2}; since ‖wSDS​𝐉𝜽⊤​𝐫‖22≤wSDS2​‖𝐉𝜽‖22​‖𝐫‖22\|w_{\textnormal{SDS}}\mathbf{J}_{{\boldsymbol{\theta}}}^{\top}\mathbf{r}\|_{2}^{2}\!\leq\!w_{\textnormal{SDS}}^{2}\|\mathbf{J}_{{\boldsymbol{\theta}}}\|_{2}^{2}\|\mathbf{r}\|_{2}^{2}, they misrank timesteps when wSDSw_{\textnormal{SDS}} or ‖𝐉𝜽‖2\|\mathbf{J}_{{\boldsymbol{\theta}}}\|_{2} vary with tt or correlate poorly with ‖𝐫‖2\|\mathbf{r}\|_{2}, and backpropagation through encoders and differentiable generators amplifies this via ill-conditioned Jacobian chains.

Empirically, wSDSw_{\textnormal{SDS}} dominates the timestep dependence of the gradient norm (App. Fig. 22), so we use the negligible-cost proposal q⁡(t)∝p⁡(t)​wSDS​(t)q(t)\!\propto\!p(t)w_{\textnormal{SDS}}(t) with likelihood-ratio correction. This closely tracks the oracle (App. Fig. 23, Sec. D.1.8) and yields ∼1.2×{\sim}1.2\times variance reduction in practice (Fig. 11).

For data attribution (Sec. 4.3), gradient norms are approximately constant across timesteps (App. Fig. 29), so uniform sampling suffices. For DMD (Sec. 4.2), the weighting function is non-monotonic with data-dependent normalization, so we focus on stratification and compute reuse.

3.1.3 Leveraging Stratified Sampling

Setup. We estimate expectations over timesteps with density p⁡(t)p(t) and Gaussian ϵ\boldsymbol{\epsilon}. We use one sample per stratum with equal-width bins, so BB strata yield BB samples, each with probability 1/B1/B. These constructions work with the re-use estimator in Eq. 13 and remain unbiased under p⁡(t)p(t).

Discrete timesteps. If t∈{0,…,T−1}t\in\{0,\dots,T{-}1\} (e.g., T=1000T{=}1000), we stratify in [0,1][0,1] using BB equal bins with one draw per bin, then snap to the nearest index; this matches the discrete grid the teacher was trained on, so the snap is a no-op when B≤TB\!\leq\!T and induces at most one quantization step otherwise. We switch between continuous [0,1][0,1] and discrete {0,…,T−1}\{0,\dots,T{-}1\} views for notation. With importance proposal qq, we stratify in [0,1][0,1] then apply inverse-CDF sampling for stratified tt.

Global stratification across all renders and re-noisings. We first consider stratified sampling, where each batch element uses a different render, and timesteps are stratified across renders. With B:=R×KB\!:=\!R\times K equal-width bins on [0,1][0,1], partition the timestep domain into 𝒮b=[(b−1)/B,b/B]\smash{\mathcal{S}_{b}=[(b-1)/B,b/B]} for b=1,…,Bb=1,\dots,B, each with probability pb=1/Bp_{b}\!=\!\nicefrac{{1}}{{B}}. The global stratified estimator is:

𝐟¯global=1/B​∑b=1B𝐟⁡(𝐱b,tb,ϵb)\smash{\bar{\mathbf{f}}_{\mathrm{global}}=\nicefrac{{1}}{{B}}\sum\nolimits_{b=1}^{B}\mathbf{f}(\mathbf{x}_{b},t_{b},\boldsymbol{\epsilon}_{b})} (14)

where tb∼𝒰⁡(𝒮b)t_{b}\!\sim\!\mathcal{U}(\mathcal{S}_{b}) and 𝐱b\mathbf{x}_{b} is a (potentially reused) render.

Per-render stratification. With re-noising, set the number of strata equal to the number of re-noisings B:=KB:=K. For each render 𝐱(r)\mathbf{x}^{(r)}, draw one timestep per bin and independent noise ϵb(r)\smash{\boldsymbol{\epsilon}^{(r)}_{b}}. The per-render contribution is:

𝐟¯strat(r)=1/B​∑b=1B𝐟⁡(𝐱(r),tb(r),ϵb(r))\smash{\bar{\mathbf{f}}^{(r)}_{\mathrm{strat}}=\nicefrac{{1}}{{B}}\sum\nolimits_{b=1}^{B}\mathbf{f}(\mathbf{x}^{(r)},t^{(r)}_{b},\boldsymbol{\epsilon}^{(r)}_{b})} (15)

where tb(r)\smash{t^{(r)}_{b}} is uniform on 𝒮b\mathcal{S}_{b}, and gradient estimate is 1R​∑r𝐟¯strat(r)​∂𝐱(r)∂𝜽\smash{\tfrac{1}{R}\sum_{r}\bar{\mathbf{f}}^{(r)}_{\mathrm{strat}}\tfrac{\partial\mathbf{x}^{(r)}}{\partial{\boldsymbol{\theta}}}} (see Eq. 13). This ensures balanced coverage of low- and high-noise bands per render. We compare global versus per-render stratification in App. Fig. 24.

Stratified importance sampling: To combine IS and stratification for a non-uniform proposal, stratify in proposal-quantile space rather than tt (Fig. 4). For each render 𝐱(r)\mathbf{x}^{(r)} and stratum b=1​…​Bb=1\dots B, with proposal q⁡(t)q(t) and IID jitters 𝝃b(r)∼𝒰⁡(0,1)\smash{\boldsymbol{\xi}^{(r)}_{b}\sim\mathcal{U}(0,1)}, define:

ub(r)=b−1+𝝃b(r)/Btb(r)=CDFq−1​(ub(r))\smash{\!\!\!\!u^{(r)}_{b}=\nicefrac{{b-1+\boldsymbol{\xi}^{(r)}_{b}}}{{B}}\quad t^{(r)}_{b}=\textnormal{CDF}_{q}^{-1}(u^{(r)}_{b})} (16)

so that {tb(r)}b=1B\smash{\{t^{(r)}_{b}\}_{b=1}^{B}} contains one draw from each equal-mass stratum of qq, or equivalently, non-uniform bins in tt whose qq-probabilities are all 1/B1/B. With independent ϵb(r)∼𝒩⁡(𝟎,𝐈)\smash{\boldsymbol{\epsilon}^{(r)}_{b}\sim\mathcal{N}(\mathbf{0},\mathbf{I})} and importance weights w~​(t)=p⁡(t)/q⁡(t)\tilde{w}(t)=\nicefrac{{p(t)}}{{q(t)}}, the per-render stratified-IS contribution is:

𝐟¯strat​-​IS(r)=1/B​∑b=1Bw~​(tb(r))​𝐟​(𝐱(r),tb(r),ϵb(r))\smash{\!\!\!\!\bar{\mathbf{f}}^{(r)}_{\mathrm{strat\mbox{-}IS}}\!=\!\nicefrac{{1}}{{B}}\!\!\sum\nolimits_{b=1}^{B}\!\!\!\tilde{w}(t^{(r)}_{b}\!)\mathbf{f}(\mathbf{x}^{(r)}\!\!,t^{(r)}_{b}\!\!,\boldsymbol{\epsilon}^{(r)}_{b}\!)} (17)

This remains unbiased for sampling t∼pt\sim p while reallocating draws toward timesteps with larger contributions via qq and reducing variance by enforcing balanced coverage across the qq-quantiles, preventing sample clustering in tt even when qq is highly non-uniform.

Stratification design choices. Both stratification schemes add negligible compute, so the question is which to use, not whether. Per-render stratification (Eq. 15) is preferred when K>1K\!>\!1, exploiting the hierarchical structure to reduce within-render variance and composing with compute reuse; when K=1K\!=\!1 it degenerates to uniform, so global stratification (Eq. 14) is the right alternative. We confirm this in App. Fig. 24 and use per-render for our experiments, where K>1K\!>\!1 is efficient.

3.2 Variance Measurement Framework

We quantify the effectiveness of the variance reduction strategies above using Welford’s online algorithm [86] to estimate the variance of our estimators (Eq. 3) without storing samples. Estimation runs until the variance estimate converges (convergence criteria in App. Sec. C.1). For some experiments, we compute a high-sample reference to validate convergence: agreement between the MSE to this reference and the online estimate confirms convergence and unbiasedness. The reference also enables cosine-similarity metrics for assessing the directional accuracy of gradient estimates.

Efficiency metrics. To compare estimators differing in both variance and cost (wall-clock), we follow the Monte Carlo literature: efficiency ∝1/(Var⋅cost)\propto 1/(\mathrm{Var}\cdot\mathrm{cost}). We report two metrics (>1>\!1 better; see App. Fig. 9 for intuition):

  • •

    Effective compute multiplier (ECM) compares to a baseline (uniform-IID with K=1K\!=\!1) at iso-variance: ECM=costbaseline/costmethod\mathrm{ECM}=\mathrm{cost}_{\mathrm{baseline}}/\mathrm{cost}_{\mathrm{method}}. Computing ECM requires estimating costbaseline\mathrm{cost}_{\mathrm{baseline}} at the method’s variance; we interpolate in log-log space along the baseline Pareto curve, exploiting the standard Monte Carlo variance rate Var∝1/R\mathrm{Var}\propto 1/R to extrapolate when needed.

  • •

    Relative efficiency (RE) compares to uniform-IID at identical (R,K)(R,K): RE=Varu/Varm\mathrm{RE}\!=\!\mathrm{Var}_{\mathrm{u}}/\mathrm{Var}_{\mathrm{m}}, isolating sampling strategy (IW, stratification) from batch-size effects.

Task-specific quantities. For SDS (Sec. 4.1), we measure variance of 𝐮^SDS​(𝜽)\hat{\mathbf{u}}_{\textnormal{SDS}}({\boldsymbol{\theta}}) estimating 𝐮SDS​(𝜽)\mathbf{u}_{\textnormal{SDS}}({\boldsymbol{\theta}}) (Eq. 8). For DMD (Sec. 4.2), we measure the variance of the generator gradient from the score difference. For data attribution (Sec. 4.3), we measure the variance of per-example gradients used for influence scores. Details in App. Sec. C.1.

4 Experiments

We apply our methods to three diffusion-teacher tasks: optimization with diffusion priors (Sec. 4.1), single-step distillation (Sec. 4.2), and data attribution (Sec. 4.3). Across tasks, our framework reveals lower-variance setups per compute budget; details in App. Sec. D.

4.1 Diffusion Priors for Optimization

Setup: We use threestudio [13] with default hyperparameters per recent work [89]. Our uniform baseline is the standard SDS configuration used in DreamFusion [58], Magic3D [29], and ProlificDreamer [85]: uniform timestep sampling on [tmin,tmax][t_{\min},t_{\max}] with one re-noising per render (K=1K\!=\!1); our methods are drop-in modifications that preserve the SDS objective. We measure: variance of SDS-latent-space updates and parameter gradients (and related dispersion); effective compute multipliers (how much baseline compute matches our variance); CLIP scores [15] for coarse prompt alignment; and equal-cost renders throughout training to contrast fidelity. Details in App. Sec. D.

Quantitative Results: Fig. 5: compute reuse alone yields ∼2.6×\sim\!2.6\times, IW+Strat ∼3.3×\sim\!3.3\times. Fig. 11 shows IW (∼−24%{\sim}14\!-\!24\%) and stratification (∼−12%{\sim}10\!-\!12\%) are complementary (∼−31%{\sim}25\!-\!31\% combined); Tables 1, 2 break this down. Fig. 7: with matched per-iteration cost across 3030 prompts and 33 seeds, IW+Strat reaches the standard-SDS baseline’s converged CLIP score in roughly half the iterations (∼2×{\sim}2\times wall-clock time for comparable quality). Per-render stratification beats global (App. Fig. 24); the weight-based IW matches the oracle (App. Fig. 23, Table 6); IW+Strat captures ∼91%{\sim}91\% of a Sinkhorn-optimal pair-probability allocation (per-snapshot, N=2N\!=\!2; App. Sec. D.1.6); the IW+Strat >> IW ≈\approx Strat >> Uniform ranking is stable across 55 prompts (App. Table 7).

Qualitative Results: Fig. 8 shows renders throughout training for two equal-budget strategies: baseline and ours, consistent with CLIP-score trends in Fig. 7. App. Fig. 12 shows final renders comparing baseline and ours.

4.2 Single-step Diffusion Distillation

Setup: We apply our methods to Distribution Matching Distillation (DMD) [94] via the Monte-Carlo estimator in Sec. 2.3.2, on top of the FastGen [53] reference implementation. We train generators on ImageNet-256 [27] using the pretrained DiT-XL/2 teacher [57]; details in App. Sec. D.2.

Results: Table 3 shows resampling cuts gradient variance by −16×3.4\!-\!16\times at matched per-step variance budget; App. Sec. D.2 reports the corresponding ∼1.5×{\sim}1.5\times wall-clock factor. Stratification adds −2.0×1.0\!-\!2.0\times at matched compute. The largest variance reduction is in parameter gradients, where combining resampling (8,16)(8,16) with stratification yields ∼32×{\sim}32\times over baseline (8,1)(8,1) (compute-aware ECM ∼20×{\sim}20\times). While variance reduction yields similar-or-better per-step FID convergence, no practical improvement remains at matched wall-clock time (App. Fig. 26, App. Fig. 25). We retain DMD as a deliberate negative result: it isolates a regime in which the Monte Carlo gradient is no longer the bottleneck, as auxiliary losses, generator-input diversity, and bilevel optimization dynamics dominate convergence. Detailed hypotheses and ablations are in App. Sec. D.2.

4.3 Data Attribution

Setup: We follow MOTIVE [87] for video data attribution, using Wan2.1-T2V-1.3B [81], a flow-matching video model that illustrates our framework’s reach beyond noise-prediction diffusion teachers (DiffSynth-Studio implementation), on VIDGEN-1M [78]; details in App. Sec. D. Data attribution computes the influence of each training datum on a query, then ranks and finetunes on the top examples. We assess unbiased gradient estimators via gradient variance and correlation between the estimator and ground-truth rankings.

Results: Fig. 6 quantifies gradient variance (top) and ranking correlation (bottom) versus gradient evaluations per data point. Variance decreases with more samples, and stratified sampling consistently beats uniform at equal budget. This yields influence rankings that better match ground-truth gradients, achieving >2×>\!2\times effective compute multiplier at reasonable budgets (Table 4). Re-noising provides less benefit here than in other tasks because encoding cost is moderate relative to denoising, and we require accurate gradients for each fixed training example rather than averaging over sampled inputs. Global stratification is most effective and substantially reduces variance in this setting.

5 Discussion

The App. covers related work (App. Sec. E), limitations (App. Sec. F.1), and future directions (App. Sec. F.2). To our knowledge, no published work in the cited frozen-teacher SDS, DMD, or attribution lines applies timestep stratification, uses explicit per-loss weights as IS proxies, or measures parameter-gradient variance per unit compute for these tasks.

When Variance Reduction Helps: CARV helps when (1) the MC gradient dominates, (2) crender+encode>cdenoisec_{\mathrm{render+encode}}>c_{\mathrm{denoise}}, and (3) variance limits convergence. In SDS, IW+Strat captures ∼91%{\sim}91\% of a Sinkhorn-optimal pair allocation (App. Sec. D.1.6, App. Fig. 20); the gain amplifies at low classifier-free guidance, with ECM rising from ∼3.3×\sim\!3.3\times at ω=100\omega\!=\!100 to ∼3.8×\sim\!3.8\times at ω=25\omega\!=\!25 on a matched (R,K)=(2,1)(R,K)\!=\!(2,1) baseline (App. Fig. 16, App. Fig. 13), translating to CLIP-score and qualitative gains across prompts and seeds (App. Sec. D.1.5). DMD (Sec. 4.2) bounds applicability when auxiliary stabilizers or input diversity bind. CARV composes with VSD [85] and SteinDreamer [83] (App. Sec. E.4, App. Sec. E.5). Cost selection: IS ∼1.2×{\sim}1.2\times, stratification ∼−3.0×{\sim}1.0\!-\!3.0\times, reuse ∼−2.6×{\sim}1.6\!-\!2.6\times when crender+encode≫cdenoisec_{\mathrm{render+encode}}\!\gg\!c_{\mathrm{denoise}} (App. Sec. F.3).

Broader Implications: The framework (Sec. 3.2) is application-agnostic wherever upstream cost dominates the denoiser; the DMD case shows the gradient-variance lever is muted when auxiliary stabilizers or input diversity bind. We offer a map of applicability, not a one-size-fits-all claim.

5.1 Conclusion

We presented CARV, a compute-aware variance-accounting framework for frozen-teacher Monte Carlo gradients, motivating a hierarchical Monte Carlo estimator with three unbiased drop-ins: timestep importance sampling, stratification, and amortized compute reuse. In our SDS and attribution settings, CARV delivers −3×2\!-\!3\times effective compute multipliers without changing the objective; in DMD, the same techniques cut gradient variance by an order of magnitude without improving downstream FID, marking the boundary where auxiliary stabilizers and input diversity, rather than MC variance, govern convergence. These simple techniques guide practitioners in allocating compute in diffusion-guided pipelines.

Appendix A Broader Impacts

Our work improves compute efficiency of pipelines that use pretrained diffusion models as frozen teachers by reducing Monte Carlo estimator variance without changing the target objective. By reallocating samples across noise levels, stratifying timesteps, and reusing expensive upstream computations, practitioners can achieve comparable gradient quality with fewer denoiser, rendering, or encoding evaluations, thereby reducing energy use and the cost of experimentation and evaluation. These techniques are general and could also reduce the cost of developing or deploying systems that generate synthetic media, which may be misused for deception or harmful content; this paper does not introduce new generative capabilities or datasets, and responsible use should follow the safety, provenance, and content policies of the underlying models. Overall, the primary expected impact is reduced compute and iteration cost for diffusion-guided optimization, distillation, and attribution, enabling more systematic variance measurement and fairer comparisons under fixed budgets.

LLM Usage

We used a large language model as a writing and engineering assistant during the preparation of this manuscript. Specifically, it was used to (i) suggest edits for clarity and concision, (ii) help reorganize prose and LaTeX for readability, and (iii) assist with routine coding tasks (e.g., debugging scripts and preparing plotting utilities). All technical contributions, methodological decisions, experimental design, and results are our own. We verified all generated suggestions and did not rely on the model for new scientific claims or conclusions.

Reproducibility

We take several steps to ensure reproducibility of our results. First, we provide complete mathematical specifications of all proposed estimators, including importance sampling (Sec. 3.1.2), stratified sampling (Sec. 3.1.3), and compute reuse (Sec. 3.1.1), with explicit equations and a combined-pipeline pseudocode (Algorithm 1) that can be directly implemented. Second, we build on established open-source codebases: threestudio [13] for SDS (Sec. 4.1), the FastGen [53] reference implementation for DMD (Sec. 4.2), and MOTIVE [87] (DiffSynth-Studio backbone) for video data attribution (Sec. 4.3); each of our estimators in Sec. 3.1 is a small change to the per-step sampling and re-noising logic in these pipelines, not a structural change to the surrounding training loop. Third, we report all experimental settings, including batch sizes, compute budgets, number of renders and re-noises, and evaluation metrics, with additional hyperparameters and implementation details provided in App. Sec. D. Fourth, our experiments average results over multiple seeds and prompts and report standard deviations to quantify uncertainty (Fig. 7). Fifth, our variance measurement framework (Sec. 3.2) uses standard techniques (Welford’s algorithm) and verifies unbiasedness by comparing the MSE and variance, enabling independent validation of our claims. A glossary of all notation is included in Sec. G to assist in understanding.

Appendix B Additional Background

B.1 Diffusion Models

B.1.1 Sampling from Diffusion Models

To sample, a pretrained latent diffusion model uses a multi-step sampler that starts from Gaussian noise and iteratively denoises. Let {tk}k=0K\{t_{k}\}_{k=0}^{K} denote a discretization of the continuous noise schedule with t0≈0t_{0}\approx 0 and tK≈Tt_{K}\approx T. The sampler initializes latent at the highest noise level, 𝐳tK∼𝒩⁡(𝟎,𝐈)\mathbf{z}_{t_{K}}\sim\mathcal{N}(\mathbf{0},\mathbf{I}), then applies a sequence of learned transitions:

𝐳tk−1∼pϕ(𝐳tk−1∣𝐳tk,tk,𝐜),k=K,…,1\mathbf{z}_{t_{k-1}}\sim p_{{\boldsymbol{\phi}}}(\mathbf{z}_{t_{k-1}}\mid\mathbf{z}_{t_{k}},t_{k},\mathbf{c}),\qquad k=K,\dots,1 (18)

where the transition kernels parametrize the denoiser ϵ^ϕ​(𝐳tk,tk,𝐜)\hat{\boldsymbol{\epsilon}}_{{\boldsymbol{\phi}}}(\mathbf{z}_{t_{k}},t_{k},\mathbf{c}) and the chosen update rule (e.g., DDPM or a DDIM-like update). The composition of these KK steps defines a stochastic generator that maps a single Gaussian seed 𝐳tK∼𝒩⁡(𝟎,𝐈)\mathbf{z}_{t_{K}}\sim\mathcal{N}(\mathbf{0},\mathbf{I}) to a clean latent 𝐳t0\mathbf{z}_{t_{0}}. In Sec. 2.3.2, we treat this KK-step procedure as the teacher and train a one-step generator G𝜽G_{{\boldsymbol{\theta}}} to match its sample distribution in a single forward pass from noise.

Classifier-free guidance. Many text-conditioned diffusion models are trained with a classifier-free guidance setup, where the conditioning 𝐜\mathbf{c} is randomly dropped during training so that a single network learns both conditional and unconditional predictions. At sampling time, the model is evaluated in both modes and combined using a scalar guidance weight ω≥0\omega\geq 0. Using our denoiser notation, the guided noise prediction is:

ϵ^ϕ​(𝐳t,t,𝐜,ω)=(+ω)​ϵ^ϕ​(𝐳t,t,𝐜)−ω​ϵ^ϕ​(𝐳t,t,𝐜=∅)\hat{\boldsymbol{\epsilon}}_{{\boldsymbol{\phi}}}(\mathbf{z}_{t},t,\mathbf{c};\omega)\!=\!(1\!+\!\omega)\hat{\boldsymbol{\epsilon}}_{{\boldsymbol{\phi}}}(\mathbf{z}_{t},t,\mathbf{c})\!-\!\omega\hat{\boldsymbol{\epsilon}}_{{\boldsymbol{\phi}}}(\mathbf{z}_{t},t,\mathbf{c}\!=\!\varnothing) (19)

where ϵ^ϕ​(𝐳t,t,𝐜)\hat{\boldsymbol{\epsilon}}_{{\boldsymbol{\phi}}}(\mathbf{z}_{t},t,\mathbf{c}) and ϵ^ϕ​(𝐳t,t,∅)\hat{\boldsymbol{\epsilon}}_{{\boldsymbol{\phi}}}(\mathbf{z}_{t},t,\varnothing) denote the conditional and unconditional outputs of the same network. The guided prediction ϵ^ϕ\hat{\boldsymbol{\epsilon}}_{{\boldsymbol{\phi}}} is used in the sampler to update 𝐳tk\mathbf{z}_{t_{k}} and appears in the SDS gradients in Sec. 2.3.1 and Sec. 4.1.

B.2 Reducing Estimator Variance

B.2.1 Importance Sampling Theory and Application to Diffusion

We expand the importance-sampling treatment of Sec. 2.2.1.

Setup. Let t∈[0,1]t\in[0,1] be a noise level with base density p⁡(t)p(t). Let 𝝃\boldsymbol{\xi} denote all other randomness (e.g., sampled input data, Gaussian noise) drawn from a conditional distribution p⁡(𝝃∣t)p(\boldsymbol{\xi}\mid t). For a vector-valued contribution 𝐟⁡(t,𝝃)\mathbf{f}(t,\boldsymbol{\xi}) such as a training gradient, define the conditional mean integrand:

𝐅⁡(t)=𝔼⁡[𝐟⁡(t,𝝃)∣t]\mathbf{F}(t)=\mathbb{E}[\mathbf{f}(t,\boldsymbol{\xi})\mid t] (20)

and its mean integrand:

𝝁=𝔼t∼p,𝝃∼p(⋅∣t)[𝐟(t,𝝃)]=𝔼t∼p[𝐅(t)]\boldsymbol{\mu}=\mathbb{E}_{t\sim p,\boldsymbol{\xi}\sim p(\cdot\mid t)}[\mathbf{f}(t,\boldsymbol{\xi})]=\mathbb{E}_{t\sim p}[\mathbf{F}(t)] (21)

Importance sampling estimator. For any proposal density q⁡(t)q(t) with q⁡(t)>0q(t)>0 whenever p⁡(t)>0p(t)>0, define the importance weight w~​(t)=p⁡(t)q⁡(t)\tilde{w}(t)=\frac{p(t)}{q(t)} and sample t(n)∼qt^{(n)}\sim q, 𝝃(n)∼p(⋅∣t(n))\boldsymbol{\xi}^{(n)}\sim p(\cdot\mid t^{(n)}). Then the following is an unbiased estimator for 𝝁\boldsymbol{\mu}:

𝝁^q=1N​∑n=1Nw~​(t(n))​𝐟​(t(n),𝝃(n))\hat{\boldsymbol{\mu}}_{q}=\frac{1}{N}\sum_{n=1}^{N}\tilde{w}(t^{(n)})\mathbf{f}(t^{(n)},\boldsymbol{\xi}^{(n)}) (22)

Variance and optimal proposals. A direct calculation gives the trace-covariance dispersion

tr⁡(Cov⁡(𝝁^q))=1N​(∫p​(t)2q⁡(t)​𝔼​[‖𝐟⁡(t,𝝃)‖22∣t]​𝑑t−‖𝝁‖22)\mathrm{tr}(\mathrm{Cov}(\hat{\boldsymbol{\mu}}_{q}))=\frac{1}{N}\left(\int\frac{p(t)^{2}}{q(t)}\mathbb{E}[\|\mathbf{f}(t,\boldsymbol{\xi})\|_{2}^{2}\mid t]\mathrm{d}t-\|\boldsymbol{\mu}\|_{2}^{2}\right) (23)

which implies the variance-minimizing proposal under this criterion

q⋆​(t)\displaystyle q^{\star}(t) ∝p⁡(t)​𝔼⁡[‖𝐟⁡(t,𝝃)‖22∣t]\displaystyle\propto p(t)\sqrt{\mathbb{E}[\|\mathbf{f}(t,\boldsymbol{\xi})\|_{2}^{2}\mid t]} (24)
=p⁡(t)​‖𝐅⁡(t)‖22+tr⁡(Cov⁡(𝐟⁡(t,𝝃)∣t))\displaystyle=p(t)\sqrt{\|\mathbf{F}(t)\|_{2}^{2}+\mathrm{tr}(\mathrm{Cov}(\mathbf{f}(t,\boldsymbol{\xi})\mid t))} (25)

see standard treatments of optimal importance sampling [65]. If 𝐟⁡(t,𝝃)\mathbf{f}(t,\boldsymbol{\xi}) is deterministic given tt, then q⋆​(t)∝p⁡(t)​‖𝐅⁡(t)‖2q^{\star}(t)\propto p(t)\|\mathbf{F}(t)\|_{2}. For a scalar integrand, this reduces to the familiar form q⋆​(t)∝p⁡(t)​|𝐅⁡(t)|q^{\star}(t)\propto p(t)|\mathbf{F}(t)|. For vector-valued 𝐅\mathbf{F}, even the oracle proposal typically does not yield zero variance because the contribution direction can vary with tt. Intuitively, importance sampling reallocates samples toward noise levels with large root-mean-square contributions and away from those with small ones.

Loss-based proxies and their limitations. Evaluating ‖𝐅⁡(t)‖2\|\mathbf{F}(t)\|_{2} in diffusion is prohibitively expensive. Several works use the squared residual (loss) as a cheap proxy for gradient magnitude in some regimes [52, 98].

Concretely, consider the per-timestep denoising loss from the weighted diffusion objective in Eq. 1. For diffusion model training, the gradient with respect to denoiser parameters ϕ{\boldsymbol{\phi}} is

𝐟⁡(t,𝝃):=∇ϕℓ=2​𝐉ϕ⊤​𝐫​ where ​𝐉ϕ=∇ϕϵ^ϕ​(𝐳t,t,𝐜)\displaystyle\mathbf{f}(t,\boldsymbol{\xi}):=\nabla_{{\boldsymbol{\phi}}}\ell=2\mathbf{J}_{{\boldsymbol{\phi}}}^{\top}\mathbf{r}\textnormal{ where }\mathbf{J}_{{\boldsymbol{\phi}}}=\nabla_{{\boldsymbol{\phi}}}\hat{\boldsymbol{\epsilon}}_{{\boldsymbol{\phi}}}(\mathbf{z}_{t},t,\mathbf{c}) (26)

Recall that the optimal importance sampling proposal from Eq. 24 requires 𝔼⁡[‖𝐟⁡(t,𝝃)‖22∣t]\sqrt{\mathbb{E}[\|\mathbf{f}(t,\boldsymbol{\xi})\|_{2}^{2}\mid t]}, which equals:

𝔼⁡[‖∇ϕℓ‖22∣t]=‖𝔼⁡[∇ϕℓ∣t]‖22+tr⁡(Cov⁡(∇ϕℓ∣t))\displaystyle\sqrt{\mathbb{E}[\|\nabla_{{\boldsymbol{\phi}}}\ell\|_{2}^{2}\mid t]}=\sqrt{\|\mathbb{E}[\nabla_{{\boldsymbol{\phi}}}\ell\mid t]\|_{2}^{2}+\mathrm{tr}(\mathrm{Cov}(\nabla_{{\boldsymbol{\phi}}}\ell\mid t))} (27)

Since estimating this is expensive, practitioners instead use the loss 𝔼⁡[ℓ∣t]=𝔼⁡[‖𝐫‖22]\sqrt{\mathbb{E}[\ell\mid t]}=\sqrt{\mathbb{E}[\|\mathbf{r}\|_{2}^{2}]} as a cheap proxy. However, for any single sample

‖∇ϕℓ‖22=4​‖𝐉ϕ⊤​𝐫‖22≤4​‖𝐉ϕ‖22​‖𝐫‖22=4​‖𝐉ϕ‖22​ℓ\displaystyle\|\nabla_{{\boldsymbol{\phi}}}\ell\|_{2}^{2}=4\|\mathbf{J}_{{\boldsymbol{\phi}}}^{\top}\mathbf{r}\|_{2}^{2}\leq 4\|\mathbf{J}_{{\boldsymbol{\phi}}}\|_{2}^{2}\|\mathbf{r}\|_{2}^{2}=4\|\mathbf{J}_{{\boldsymbol{\phi}}}\|_{2}^{2}\ell (28)

Equality holds when 𝐫\mathbf{r} aligns with the leading left singular vector of 𝐉ϕ\mathbf{J}_{{\boldsymbol{\phi}}}. The loss proxy ℓ\ell captures only ‖𝐫‖22\|\mathbf{r}\|_{2}^{2} and ignores ‖𝐉ϕ‖22\|\mathbf{J}_{{\boldsymbol{\phi}}}\|_{2}^{2}, so a loss-derived schedule misranks timesteps whenever ‖𝐉ϕ‖2\|\mathbf{J}_{{\boldsymbol{\phi}}}\|_{2} varies with tt or correlates weakly with ‖𝐫‖2\|\mathbf{r}\|_{2}.

The gap in SDS-style optimization. This gap is amplified in the settings we focus on, where the gradient of interest is not with respect to denoiser parameters. For example, in SDS-style optimization (detailed in Sec. 2.3.1), we optimize parameters 𝜽{\boldsymbol{\theta}} of a differentiable generator using a frozen diffusion teacher. The per-timestep update takes the form:

𝐅⁡(t)\displaystyle\mathbf{F}(t) ∝w⁡(t)​𝐉𝜽⊤​𝐫​ where\displaystyle\propto w(t)\mathbf{J}_{{\boldsymbol{\theta}}}^{\top}\mathbf{r}\textnormal{ where } (29)
𝐉𝜽\displaystyle\mathbf{J}_{{\boldsymbol{\theta}}} =∇𝜽ϵ^ϕ​(𝐳t,t,𝐜)≈∇𝐱Encode​∇𝜽g\displaystyle=\nabla_{{\boldsymbol{\theta}}}\hat{\boldsymbol{\epsilon}}_{{\boldsymbol{\phi}}}(\mathbf{z}_{t},t,\mathbf{c})\approx\nabla_{\mathbf{x}}\textnormal{Encode}\nabla_{{\boldsymbol{\theta}}}g (30)

for a known scalar weight w⁡(t)w(t). Here g⁡(𝜽)g({\boldsymbol{\theta}}) is the generator output (e.g., a rendered image), Encode maps it to latent space, and the ≈\approx holds because SDS drops the teacher input Jacobian ∇𝐳ϵ^ϕ\nabla_{\mathbf{z}}\hat{\boldsymbol{\epsilon}}_{{\boldsymbol{\phi}}}. The effective Jacobian 𝐉𝜽\mathbf{J}_{{\boldsymbol{\theta}}} thus includes a potentially ill-conditioned encoder-generator chain whose timestep dependence can differ from ‖𝐫‖2\|\mathbf{r}\|_{2}. Combined with w⁡(t)w(t), this leaves room for proposals that target gradient contributions rather than the loss proxy.

Stratified-IS unbiasedness (Eq. 17). We verify that the construction in Sec. 3.1.3 yields an unbiased estimator of 𝔼t∼p​[𝐅​(t)]\mathbb{E}_{t\sim p}[\mathbf{F}(t)]. Let FqF_{q} be the CDF of the importance proposal qq and partition [0,1][0,1] into BB equal-mass strata in qq-quantile space, 𝒮b={t:Fq​(t)∈[(b−1)/B,b/B]}\mathcal{S}_{b}=\{t:F_{q}(t)\in[(b{-}1)/B,b/B]\}, so that Prt∼q[t∈𝒮b]=1/B\Pr_{t\sim q}[t\in\mathcal{S}_{b}]=1/B and the conditional density is q(t∣𝒮b)=Bq(t)𝟏[t∈𝒮b]q(t\mid\mathcal{S}_{b})=B\,q(t)\mathbf{1}[t\in\mathcal{S}_{b}]. Drawing 𝝃b∼𝒰⁡(0,1)\boldsymbol{\xi}_{b}\sim\mathcal{U}(0,1) and setting tb=Fq−1​((b−1+𝝃b)/B)t_{b}=F_{q}^{-1}((b{-}1+\boldsymbol{\xi}_{b})/B) gives tbt_{b} distributed according to q(⋅∣𝒮b)q(\cdot\mid\mathcal{S}_{b}). With importance weight w~​(t)=p​(t)/q​(t)\tilde{w}(t)=p(t)/q(t) and contribution 𝐟⁡(tb,𝝃b′)\mathbf{f}(t_{b},\boldsymbol{\xi}^{\prime}_{b}) for 𝝃b′∼p(⋅∣tb)\boldsymbol{\xi}^{\prime}_{b}\sim p(\cdot\mid t_{b}), the per-stratum expectation is

𝔼⁡[w~​(tb)​𝐟​(tb,𝝃b′)]=∫𝒮bp⁡(t)q⁡(t)​𝐅​(t)​B​q​(t)​𝑑t=B​∫𝒮bp⁡(t)​𝐅​(t)​𝑑t.\displaystyle\mathbb{E}\big[\tilde{w}(t_{b})\,\mathbf{f}(t_{b},\boldsymbol{\xi}^{\prime}_{b})\big]=\int_{\mathcal{S}_{b}}\!\frac{p(t)}{q(t)}\,\mathbf{F}(t)\,B\,q(t)\mathrm{d}t=B\!\int_{\mathcal{S}_{b}}\!p(t)\,\mathbf{F}(t)\mathrm{d}t. (31)

Averaging over the BB strata,

𝔼⁡[1B​∑b=1Bw~​(tb)​𝐟​(tb,𝝃b′)]=∑b=1B∫𝒮bp⁡(t)​𝐅​(t)​𝑑t=∫01p⁡(t)​𝐅​(t)​𝑑t=𝔼t∼p​[𝐅⁡(t)],\displaystyle\mathbb{E}\Big[\tfrac{1}{B}\!\sum_{b=1}^{B}\tilde{w}(t_{b})\,\mathbf{f}(t_{b},\boldsymbol{\xi}^{\prime}_{b})\Big]=\sum_{b=1}^{B}\int_{\mathcal{S}_{b}}\!p(t)\,\mathbf{F}(t)\mathrm{d}t=\int_{0}^{1}p(t)\,\mathbf{F}(t)\mathrm{d}t=\mathbb{E}_{t\sim p}[\mathbf{F}(t)], (32)

so Eq. 17 is unbiased for 𝔼t∼p​[𝐅​(t)]\mathbb{E}_{t\sim p}[\mathbf{F}(t)] for any proposal qq that satisfies q⁡(t)>0q(t){>}0 wherever p⁡(t)>0p(t){>}0. The variance-reduction argument follows from the standard stratified-sampling decomposition: the variance of the per-stratum-averaged estimator equals 1B\tfrac{1}{B} times the average within-stratum conditional variance (dropping the between-stratum component carried by simple Monte Carlo; Thompson [80]), composed with the usual importance-reweighting variance formula.

B.2.2 Diffusion Model Noise Schedules

We provide additional details on the connection between noise schedules and importance sampling in diffusion training, expanding on Sec. 2.2.1.

Following Kingma et al. [25], we view the noise schedule as a monotonically decreasing function

λ=fλ​(t),t∈[0,1]\lambda=f_{\lambda}(t),\qquad t\in[0,1] (33)

that maps continuous time to log signal-to-noise ratio λ=log⁡(αt2/σt2)\lambda=\log(\alpha_{t}^{2}/\sigma_{t}^{2}). Monotonicity ensures invertibility, so there is a bijection between time and logSNR.

Induced distribution over noise levels. When sampling time uniformly t∼𝒰⁡(0,1)t\sim\mathcal{U}(0,1) and evaluating λ=fλ​(t)\lambda=f_{\lambda}(t), the change-of-variables formula gives a distribution over noise levels

p⁡(λ)=|d​λd​t|−1p(\lambda)=\left|\frac{\mathrm{d}\lambda}{\mathrm{d}t}\right|^{-1} (34)

where the absolute value accounts for the fact that λ\lambda decreases with tt. Different schedules (linear, cosine, learned) induce different distributions p⁡(λ)p(\lambda) even though all sample tt uniformly.

Noise schedules as importance sampling. Changing variables from tt to λ\lambda in the weighted objective from Eq. 1, we obtain

ℒwDiff​(ϕ)=12​∫λminλmaxw⁡(λ)​𝔼ϵ​[‖ϵ^ϕ​(𝐳λ,λ,𝐜)−ϵ‖22]​𝑑λ\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{wDiff}}({\boldsymbol{\phi}})=\tfrac{1}{2}\int_{\lambda_{\min}}^{\lambda_{\max}}w(\lambda)\mathbb{E}_{\boldsymbol{\epsilon}}\left[\|\hat{\boldsymbol{\epsilon}}_{{\boldsymbol{\phi}}}(\mathbf{z}_{\lambda},\lambda,\mathbf{c})-\boldsymbol{\epsilon}\|_{2}^{2}\right]\mathrm{d}\lambda (35)

where λmin=fλ​(1)\lambda_{\min}=f_{\lambda}(1) and λmax=fλ​(0)\lambda_{\max}=f_{\lambda}(0) are the schedule endpoints and 𝐳λ\mathbf{z}_{\lambda} denotes the encoded data noised to level λ\lambda. This integral does not depend on the schedule fλf_{\lambda} except through the endpoints.

Equivalently, we can write the objective as an expectation over the induced distribution p⁡(λ)p(\lambda):

ℒwDiff​(ϕ)=12​𝔼λ∼p⁡(λ),ϵ∼𝒩⁡(𝟎,𝐈)​[w⁡(λ)p⁡(λ)​‖ϵ^ϕ​(𝐳λ,λ,𝐜)−ϵ‖22]\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{wDiff}}({\boldsymbol{\phi}})=\tfrac{1}{2}\mathbb{E}_{\lambda\sim p(\lambda),\boldsymbol{\epsilon}\sim\mathcal{N}(\mathbf{0},\mathbf{I})}\left[\frac{w(\lambda)}{p(\lambda)}\|\hat{\boldsymbol{\epsilon}}_{{\boldsymbol{\phi}}}(\mathbf{z}_{\lambda},\lambda,\mathbf{c})-\boldsymbol{\epsilon}\|_{2}^{2}\right] (36)

The noise schedule thus induces an importance distribution p⁡(λ)p(\lambda) over noise levels. ℒwDiff\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{wDiff}} is invariant to the schedule (up to endpoints), but estimator variance depends on how p⁡(λ)p(\lambda) aligns with the integrand: schedule design for diffusion-model training is an importance-sampling problem.

Schedules versus weights in downstream applications. In SDS and DMD (Secs. 2.3.1, 2.3.2), practitioners inherit a fixed teacher schedule and apply an additional weight w⁡(t)w(t) or wSDS​(t)w_{\textnormal{SDS}}(t) that conflates the intrinsic loss weight w⁡(λ)w(\lambda) with the schedule-induced density p⁡(λ)p(\lambda). The SDS weight wSDS​(t)w_{\textnormal{SDS}}(t) typically bundles modeling choices (e.g., αt\alpha_{t}) with implicit timestep reweighting; if monotonic, it induces a new effective timestep distribution. DMD’s weighting involves data-dependent normalization (e.g., ‖𝝁base​(𝐳t,t)−𝐳‖\|\boldsymbol{\mu}_{\mathrm{base}}(\mathbf{z}_{t},t)-\mathbf{z}\|) and is non-monotonic, so it does not map to a simple schedule. Sec. 3.1.2 treats these weights as known functions, building proposals q⁡(t)q(t) via likelihood ratios to avoid conflating schedule and reweighting.

B.3 Diffusion Model Applications

B.3.1 Diffusion Priors for Optimization

Score Distillation Sampling (SDS) uses a pretrained diffusion model over an observation space (images, videos, audio, or latents) as a frozen conditional prior that supplies gradients to a parametrized generator, renderer, or simulator. Given parameters 𝜽{\boldsymbol{\theta}} and a sampled rendering condition 𝐪\mathbf{q} (for example, camera pose in text-to-3D), we render an observation

𝐳=g⁡(𝜽,𝐪)=Encode​(g′​(𝜽,𝐪)),\displaystyle\mathbf{z}=g({\boldsymbol{\theta}},\mathbf{q})=\textnormal{Encode}\!\big(g^{\prime}({\boldsymbol{\theta}},\mathbf{q})\big), (37)

where g′g^{\prime} is a (possibly non-latent) render and Encode maps into the teacher’s observation space (often latent). We update 𝜽{\boldsymbol{\theta}} so 𝐳\mathbf{z} lies in high-density regions of pϕ(⋅∣𝐜)p_{{\boldsymbol{\phi}}}(\cdot\mid\mathbf{c}) (with optional guidance), giving the chain rule

∇𝜽𝔼𝐪​[log⁡pϕ​(g⁡(𝜽,𝐪)∣𝐜)]=𝔼𝐪[d​log⁡pϕ​(𝐳∣𝐜)d​𝐳​d​𝐳d​𝜽].\displaystyle\nabla_{{\boldsymbol{\theta}}}\,\Eop_{\mathbf{q}}\!\left[\log p_{{\boldsymbol{\phi}}}(g({\boldsymbol{\theta}},\mathbf{q})\mid\mathbf{c})\right]=\Eop_{\mathbf{q}}\!\left[\frac{\mathrm{d}\log p_{{\boldsymbol{\phi}}}(\mathbf{z}\mid\mathbf{c})}{\mathrm{d}\mathbf{z}}\frac{\mathrm{d}\mathbf{z}}{\mathrm{d}{\boldsymbol{\theta}}}\right]. (38)

Diffusion teacher and the SDS residual. Write the forward noising process (in the teacher’s observation space) as

𝐳t=𝐳t​(𝐳,t,ϵ)=αt​𝐳+σt​ϵ,ϵ∼𝒩⁡(0,𝐈),t∼q⁡(t),\displaystyle\mathbf{z}_{t}=\mathbf{z}_{t}(\mathbf{z},t,\boldsymbol{\epsilon})=\alpha_{t}\,\mathbf{z}+\sigma_{t}\,\boldsymbol{\epsilon},\qquad\boldsymbol{\epsilon}\sim\mathcal{N}(0,\mathbf{I}),\qquad t\sim q(t), (39)

where αt,σt\alpha_{t},\sigma_{t} are the usual diffusion coefficients (the exact parameterization is model-dependent). Let the teacher predict noise (optionally with classifier-free guidance scale ω\omega):

ϵ^ϕ=ϵ^ϕ​(𝐳t,t,𝐜,ω).\displaystyle\hat{\boldsymbol{\epsilon}}_{{\boldsymbol{\phi}}}=\hat{\boldsymbol{\epsilon}}_{{\boldsymbol{\phi}}}(\mathbf{z}_{t},t,\mathbf{c};\omega). (40)

We define the per-sample denoising residual

𝐫ϕ​(𝜽,𝐪,t,ϵ,𝐜,ω):=ϵ^ϕ​(𝐳t,t,𝐜,ω)−ϵ,\displaystyle\mathbf{r}_{\!{\boldsymbol{\phi}}}\!({\boldsymbol{\theta}},\mathbf{q},t,\boldsymbol{\epsilon},\mathbf{c},\omega):=\hat{\boldsymbol{\epsilon}}_{{\boldsymbol{\phi}}}(\mathbf{z}_{t},t,\mathbf{c};\omega)-\boldsymbol{\epsilon}, (41)

where 𝐳t\mathbf{z}_{t} is understood to be 𝐳t​(𝐳⁡(𝜽,𝐪),t,ϵ)\mathbf{z}_{t}(\mathbf{z}({\boldsymbol{\theta}},\mathbf{q}),t,\boldsymbol{\epsilon}).

SDS gradient estimator (with stop-gradient through the teacher). SDS uses a simple surrogate for the score term d​log⁡pϕ​(𝐳∣𝐜)/d​𝐳\mathrm{d}\log p_{{\boldsymbol{\phi}}}(\mathbf{z}\mid\mathbf{c})/\mathrm{d}\mathbf{z} by differentiating through the noising map but not through the teacher prediction. Concretely, in the backward pass we treat ϵ^ϕ​(⋅)\hat{\boldsymbol{\epsilon}}_{{\boldsymbol{\phi}}}(\cdot) as a constant with respect to 𝐳t\mathbf{z}_{t} (equivalently, we drop the Jacobian d​ϵ^ϕ/d​𝐳t\mathrm{d}\hat{\boldsymbol{\epsilon}}_{{\boldsymbol{\phi}}}/\mathrm{d}\mathbf{z}_{t}). This yields the estimator

𝐮SDS​(𝜽)=𝔼𝐪[𝔼t∼q⁡(t),ϵ∼𝒩⁡(0,I)[wSDS​(t)​sg⁡(𝐫ϕ)​d​𝐳td​𝐳]​d​𝐳d​𝜽].\displaystyle\mathbf{u}_{\textnormal{SDS}}({\boldsymbol{\theta}})=\Eop_{\mathbf{q}}\!\left[\Eop_{t\sim q(t),\,\boldsymbol{\epsilon}\sim\mathcal{N}(0,I)}\!\left[w_{\textnormal{SDS}}(t)\,\operatorname{sg}\!\big(\mathbf{r}_{\!{\boldsymbol{\phi}}}\big)\,\frac{\mathrm{d}\mathbf{z}_{t}}{\mathrm{d}\mathbf{z}}\right]\frac{\mathrm{d}\mathbf{z}}{\mathrm{d}{\boldsymbol{\theta}}}\right]. (42)

Here wSDS​(t)w_{\textnormal{SDS}}(t) is a scalar weight that absorbs the diffusion-dependent scaling used by SDS, and, in our implementation, can also absorb d​𝐳t/d​𝐳\mathrm{d}\mathbf{z}_{t}/\mathrm{d}\mathbf{z}). Under Eq. 39, d​𝐳t/d​𝐳=αt​𝐈\mathrm{d}\mathbf{z}_{t}/\mathrm{d}\mathbf{z}=\alpha_{t}\mathbf{I}, so Eq. 8 matches the common implementation pattern where the timestep weight includes the αt\alpha_{t} factor.

Equivalent surrogate MSE form used in code. The same update can be obtained as the gradient of a mean-squared error objective with a stop-gradient target. Define the (detached) per-sample gradient direction in observation space

g^𝐳:=wSDS​(t)​sg⁡(𝐫ϕ)\displaystyle\widehat{g}_{\mathbf{z}}:=w_{\textnormal{SDS}}(t)\,\operatorname{sg}\!\big(\mathbf{r}_{\!{\boldsymbol{\phi}}}\big)\, (43)

and set the target as

𝐳tgt:=sg⁡(𝐳−g^𝐳).\displaystyle\mathbf{z}_{\text{tgt}}:=\operatorname{sg}\!\left(\mathbf{z}-\widehat{g}_{\mathbf{z}}\right). (44)

Then the surrogate loss

ℒSDS​(𝜽):=12​𝔼𝐪,t,ϵ[‖𝐳⁡(𝜽,𝐪)−𝐳tgt‖22]\displaystyle\mathcal{L}_{\text{SDS}}({\boldsymbol{\theta}}):=\tfrac{1}{2}\,\Eop_{\mathbf{q},t,\boldsymbol{\epsilon}}\!\left[\left\|\mathbf{z}({\boldsymbol{\theta}},\mathbf{q})-\mathbf{z}_{\text{tgt}}\right\|_{2}^{2}\right] (45)

has gradient

∇𝜽ℒSDS​(𝜽)=𝔼𝐪,t,ϵ[g^𝐳​d​𝐳d​𝜽],\displaystyle\nabla_{{\boldsymbol{\theta}}}\mathcal{L}_{\text{SDS}}({\boldsymbol{\theta}})=\Eop_{\mathbf{q},t,\boldsymbol{\epsilon}}\!\left[\widehat{g}_{\mathbf{z}}\,\frac{\mathrm{d}\mathbf{z}}{\mathrm{d}{\boldsymbol{\theta}}}\right], (46)

which matches Eq. 8. This is the form we implement: we compute g^𝐳\widehat{g}_{\mathbf{z}} using the frozen teacher (with stop-gradient through ϵ^ϕ\hat{\boldsymbol{\epsilon}}_{{\boldsymbol{\phi}}} and forward noising), form the detached target Eq. 44, and optimize the MSE Eq. 45.

B.3.2 Single-Step Diffusion Distillation

We derive Distribution Matching Distillation (DMD) and connect it to our framework.

Objective and score-based formulation. DMD distills a pretrained multi-step diffusion teacher into a one-step generator G𝜽:ℝd→ℝdG_{{\boldsymbol{\theta}}}:\mathbb{R}^{d}\to\mathbb{R}^{d} parameterized by 𝜽{\boldsymbol{\theta}}. Given ϵ∼𝒩⁡(𝟎,𝐈)\boldsymbol{\epsilon}\sim\mathcal{N}(\mathbf{0},\mathbf{I}), the generator produces 𝐳=G𝜽​(ϵ)\mathbf{z}=G_{{\boldsymbol{\theta}}}(\boldsymbol{\epsilon}) and induces a distribution pfake​(𝐳)p_{\mathrm{fake}}(\mathbf{z}). The goal is to match pfakep_{\mathrm{fake}} to the real data distribution prealp_{\mathrm{real}} by minimizing the reverse KL divergence:

DKL(pfake∥preal)=𝔼𝐳∼pfake[logpfake(𝐳)−logpreal(𝐳)]D_{\mathrm{KL}}(p_{\mathrm{fake}}\|p_{\mathrm{real}})=\mathbb{E}_{\mathbf{z}\sim p_{\mathrm{fake}}}[\log p_{\mathrm{fake}}(\mathbf{z})-\log p_{\mathrm{real}}(\mathbf{z})] (47)

Taking the gradient with respect to 𝜽{\boldsymbol{\theta}} and applying the chain rule gives:

∇𝜽DKL(pfake∥preal)=𝔼ϵ∼𝒩⁡(𝟎,𝐈)[(𝐬fake(𝐳)−𝐬real(𝐳))∂G𝜽​(ϵ)∂𝜽]\nabla_{\boldsymbol{\theta}}D_{\mathrm{KL}}(p_{\mathrm{fake}}\|p_{\mathrm{real}})=\mathbb{E}_{\boldsymbol{\epsilon}\sim\mathcal{N}(\mathbf{0},\mathbf{I})}[(\mathbf{s}_{\mathrm{fake}}(\mathbf{z})-\mathbf{s}_{\mathrm{real}}(\mathbf{z}))\tfrac{\partial G_{{\boldsymbol{\theta}}}(\boldsymbol{\epsilon})}{\partial{\boldsymbol{\theta}}}] (48)

where 𝐳=G𝜽​(ϵ)\mathbf{z}=G_{{\boldsymbol{\theta}}}(\boldsymbol{\epsilon}) and the score functions are 𝐬real​(𝐳)=∇𝐳​log​preal​(𝐳)\mathbf{s}_{\mathrm{real}}(\mathbf{z})=\nabla_{\mathbf{z}}\log p_{\mathrm{real}}(\mathbf{z}) and 𝐬fake​(𝐳)=∇𝐳​log​pfake​(𝐳)\mathbf{s}_{\mathrm{fake}}(\mathbf{z})=\nabla_{\mathbf{z}}\log p_{\mathrm{fake}}(\mathbf{z}).

Score estimation via diffusion noising. Direct score evaluation is intractable and unstable when pfakep_{\mathrm{fake}} and prealp_{\mathrm{real}} have disjoint support. DMD estimates scores by perturbing samples with forward diffusion noise and denoising them with diffusion models. For a clean sample 𝐳\mathbf{z} and timestep tt, form the noised sample:

𝐳t=αt​𝐳+σt​ϵ′,ϵ′∼𝒩⁡(𝟎,𝐈)\mathbf{z}_{t}=\alpha_{t}\mathbf{z}+\sigma_{t}\boldsymbol{\epsilon}^{\prime},\qquad\boldsymbol{\epsilon}^{\prime}\sim\mathcal{N}(\mathbf{0},\mathbf{I}) (49)

where αt,σt\alpha_{t},\sigma_{t} are the same diffusion schedule coefficients used in Sec. 2.1. The score of the noised distribution can be related to a denoising mean predictor. If 𝝁⁡(𝐳t,t)\boldsymbol{\mu}(\mathbf{z}_{t},t) predicts 𝔼[𝐳∣𝐳t,t]\mathbb{E}[\mathbf{z}\mid\mathbf{z}_{t},t], then:

∇𝐳t​log​p​(𝐳t∣t)=−𝐳t−αt​𝝁​(𝐳t,t)σt2\nabla_{\mathbf{z}_{t}}\log p(\mathbf{z}_{t}\mid t)=-\frac{\mathbf{z}_{t}-\alpha_{t}\boldsymbol{\mu}(\mathbf{z}_{t},t)}{\sigma_{t}^{2}} (50)

DMD uses two mean predictors:

  • •

    𝝁base​(𝐳t,t)\boldsymbol{\mu}_{\mathrm{base}}(\mathbf{z}_{t},t): the frozen pretrained teacher, estimates 𝔼[𝐳∣𝐳t,t]\mathbb{E}[\mathbf{z}\mid\mathbf{z}_{t},t] under prealp_{\mathrm{real}}

  • •

    𝝁fakeϕ​(𝐳t,t)\boldsymbol{\mu}_{\mathrm{fake}}^{{\boldsymbol{\phi}}}(\mathbf{z}_{t},t): a learned model parameterized by ϕ{\boldsymbol{\phi}}, estimates 𝔼[𝐳∣𝐳t,t]\mathbb{E}[\mathbf{z}\mid\mathbf{z}_{t},t] under pfakep_{\mathrm{fake}}

The approximate scores are:

𝐬real​(𝐳t,t)\displaystyle\mathbf{s}_{\mathrm{real}}(\mathbf{z}_{t},t) =−𝐳t−αt​𝝁base​(𝐳t,t)σt2\displaystyle=-\frac{\mathbf{z}_{t}-\alpha_{t}\boldsymbol{\mu}_{\mathrm{base}}(\mathbf{z}_{t},t)}{\sigma_{t}^{2}} (51)
𝐬fake​(𝐳t,t)\displaystyle\mathbf{s}_{\mathrm{fake}}(\mathbf{z}_{t},t) =−𝐳t−αt​𝝁fakeϕ​(𝐳t,t)σt2\displaystyle=-\frac{\mathbf{z}_{t}-\alpha_{t}\boldsymbol{\mu}_{\mathrm{fake}}^{{\boldsymbol{\phi}}}(\mathbf{z}_{t},t)}{\sigma_{t}^{2}}

Noising ensures that both distributions have overlapping support in 𝐳t\mathbf{z}_{t}-space, stabilizing training.

Practical gradient estimator. Substituting the noised-score approximations and integrating over timesteps gives the DMD generator gradient:

∇𝜽DKL≃𝔼ϵ∼𝒩⁡(𝟎,𝐈)t∼p⁡(t)ϵ′∼𝒩⁡(𝟎,𝐈)[w⁡(t)​αt​(𝐬fake​(𝐳t,t)−𝐬real​(𝐳t,t))×∂G𝜽​(ϵ)∂𝜽]\displaystyle\nabla_{\boldsymbol{\theta}}D_{\mathrm{KL}}\simeq\Eop_{\begin{subarray}{c}\boldsymbol{\epsilon}\sim\mathcal{N}(\mathbf{0},\mathbf{I})\\ t\sim p(t)\\ \boldsymbol{\epsilon}^{\prime}\sim\mathcal{N}(\mathbf{0},\mathbf{I})\end{subarray}}\bigg[w(t)\alpha_{t}\left(\mathbf{s}_{\mathrm{fake}}(\mathbf{z}_{t},t)-\mathbf{s}_{\mathrm{real}}(\mathbf{z}_{t},t)\right)\times\tfrac{\partial G_{{\boldsymbol{\theta}}}(\boldsymbol{\epsilon})}{\partial{\boldsymbol{\theta}}}\bigg] (52)

where 𝐳=G𝜽​(ϵ)\mathbf{z}=G_{{\boldsymbol{\theta}}}(\boldsymbol{\epsilon}), 𝐳t=αt​𝐳+σt​ϵ′\mathbf{z}_{t}=\alpha_{t}\mathbf{z}+\sigma_{t}\boldsymbol{\epsilon}^{\prime}, and w⁡(t)w(t) is a weighting function. A common choice is:

w⁡(t)=σt2αt​C​S‖𝝁base​(𝐳t,t)−𝐳‖1w(t)=\frac{\sigma_{t}^{2}}{\alpha_{t}}\frac{CS}{\|\boldsymbol{\mu}_{\mathrm{base}}(\mathbf{z}_{t},t)-\mathbf{z}\|_{1}} (53)

where CC and SS are the number of channels and spatial locations. This weight normalizes scale variations across timesteps. Intuitively, 𝐬real\mathbf{s}_{\mathrm{real}} pulls generator samples toward the data manifold, while −𝐬fake-\mathbf{s}_{\mathrm{fake}} discourages mode collapse by repelling samples from regions of excessive fake density.

Auxiliary losses. To track the evolving fake distribution during training, DMD updates 𝝁fakeϕ\boldsymbol{\mu}_{\mathrm{fake}}^{{\boldsymbol{\phi}}} online using a standard diffusion denoising loss on stop-gradient generator outputs:

ℒdenoise​(ϕ)=𝔼ϵ,t,ϵ′[‖𝝁fakeϕ​(𝐳t,t)−sg⁡(𝐳)‖22]\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{denoise}}({\boldsymbol{\phi}})=\Eop_{\boldsymbol{\epsilon},t,\boldsymbol{\epsilon}^{\prime}}\left[\|\boldsymbol{\mu}_{\mathrm{fake}}^{{\boldsymbol{\phi}}}(\mathbf{z}_{t},t)-\operatorname{sg}(\mathbf{z})\|_{2}^{2}\right] (54)

where 𝐳=G𝜽​(ϵ)\mathbf{z}=G_{{\boldsymbol{\theta}}}(\boldsymbol{\epsilon}) and 𝐳t=αt​𝐳+σt​ϵ′\mathbf{z}_{t}=\alpha_{t}\mathbf{z}+\sigma_{t}\boldsymbol{\epsilon}^{\prime}.

Additionally, an optional regression loss aligns the one-step generator with deterministic samples from the teacher on a small paired dataset 𝒟={(𝐱,𝐲)}\mathcal{D}=\{(\mathbf{x},\mathbf{y})\}:

ℒreg​(𝜽)=𝔼(𝐱,𝐲)∼𝒟​[ℓ⁡(G𝜽​(𝐱),𝐲)]\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{reg}}({\boldsymbol{\theta}})=\mathbb{E}_{(\mathbf{x},\mathbf{y})\sim\mathcal{D}}\left[\ell(G_{{\boldsymbol{\theta}}}(\mathbf{x}),\mathbf{y})\right] (55)

where ℓ\ell is a perceptual distance such as LPIPS. As in Yin et al. [93], we do not use this loss in our experiments. Yin et al. [93] also introduced a discriminator trained on the fake model’s features to distinguish data from the generator or teacher distributions. We also utilize this objective in our experiments. The generator is trained with the combined objective while the fake model minimizes ℒdenoise​(ϕ)\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{denoise}}({\boldsymbol{\phi}}) and remains detached in the generator gradient.

Classifier-free guidance. For conditional generation with text conditioning 𝐜\mathbf{c} and classifier-free guidance scale ω\omega, the same construction applies. The real score uses the guided teacher prediction:

𝝁base​(𝐳t,t,𝐜,ω)=(1+ω)​𝝁base​(𝐳t,t,𝐜)−ω​𝝁base​(𝐳t,t,∅)\boldsymbol{\mu}_{\mathrm{base}}(\mathbf{z}_{t},t,\mathbf{c};\omega)=(1+\omega)\boldsymbol{\mu}_{\mathrm{base}}(\mathbf{z}_{t},t,\mathbf{c})-\omega\boldsymbol{\mu}_{\mathrm{base}}(\mathbf{z}_{t},t,\varnothing) (56)

while the fake score is unchanged. The generator trains at a fixed guidance scale to match the guided teacher distribution.

Connection to variance reduction. The DMD gradient is a Monte Carlo expectation over three sources of randomness: generator input ϵ\boldsymbol{\epsilon}, timestep tt, and forward noise ϵ′\boldsymbol{\epsilon}^{\prime}. Each gradient sample requires:

  1. 1.

    Generating 𝐳=G𝜽​(ϵ)\mathbf{z}=G_{{\boldsymbol{\theta}}}(\boldsymbol{\epsilon}) (potentially expensive)

  2. 2.

    Forward noising to form 𝐳t\mathbf{z}_{t} (cheap)

  3. 3.

    Evaluating both 𝝁base\boldsymbol{\mu}_{\mathrm{base}} and 𝝁fakeϕ\boldsymbol{\mu}_{\mathrm{fake}}^{{\boldsymbol{\phi}}} (moderate cost)

  4. 4.

    Backpropagating through G𝜽G_{{\boldsymbol{\theta}}} (expensive)

Since step (1) is independent of (t,ϵ′)(t,\boldsymbol{\epsilon}^{\prime}), the amortized resampling strategy from Sec. 3.1.1 can cache 𝐳=G𝜽​(ϵ)\mathbf{z}=G_{{\boldsymbol{\theta}}}(\boldsymbol{\epsilon}) and resample (t,ϵ′)(t,\boldsymbol{\epsilon}^{\prime}) multiple times per generator forward pass. Similarly, timestep stratification (Sec. 3.1.3) and importance sampling (Sec. 3.1.2) reduce variance over tt. Unlike SDS, generator input variability often dominates in DMD, so allocating budget to more independent samples ϵ\boldsymbol{\epsilon} (rather than many re-noisings per sample) can be more effective, as discussed in Sec. 4.2.

B.3.3 Data Attribution for Video Generation

We summarize influence-function attribution, common scalable approximations, and the diffusion- and video-specific details needed to connect attribution to our estimator-variance framework.

Influence functions and scalable approximations. Let ℒ⁡(ϕ,𝐱,𝐜)\mathcal{L}({\boldsymbol{\phi}};\mathbf{x},\mathbf{c}) be a per-example training loss with query (𝐱query,𝐜query)(\mathbf{x}_{\mathrm{query}},\mathbf{c}_{\mathrm{query}}). For training example (𝐱n,𝐜n)(\mathbf{x}_{n},\mathbf{c}_{n}), upweighting it changes the query loss (under regularity) as [26]

I⁡((𝐱n,𝐜n),(𝐱query,𝐜query))=−∇ϕℒ​(ϕ,𝐱query,𝐜query)⊤​𝐇​(ϕ)−1​∇ϕℒ​(ϕ,𝐱n,𝐜n)I((\mathbf{x}_{n},\mathbf{c}_{n}),(\mathbf{x}_{\mathrm{query}},\mathbf{c}_{\mathrm{query}}))=-\nabla_{{\boldsymbol{\phi}}}\mathcal{L}({\boldsymbol{\phi}};\mathbf{x}_{\mathrm{query}},\mathbf{c}_{\mathrm{query}})^{\top}\mathbf{H}({\boldsymbol{\phi}})^{-1}\nabla_{{\boldsymbol{\phi}}}\mathcal{L}({\boldsymbol{\phi}};\mathbf{x}_{n},\mathbf{c}_{n}) (57)

where 𝐇⁡(ϕ)=∇ϕ21|𝒟|​∑(𝐱,𝐜)∈𝒟ℒ⁡(ϕ,𝐱,𝐜)\mathbf{H}({\boldsymbol{\phi}})=\nabla_{{\boldsymbol{\phi}}}^{2}\frac{1}{|\mathcal{D}|}\sum_{(\mathbf{x},\mathbf{c})\in\mathcal{D}}\mathcal{L}({\boldsymbol{\phi}};\mathbf{x},\mathbf{c}). Since applying 𝐇​(ϕ)−1\mathbf{H}({\boldsymbol{\phi}})^{-1} is infeasible at modern scales, practical methods approximate influence using gradient similarity computed across checkpoints (TracIn) or via projected gradient features (TRAK) [59, 55].

Diffusion attribution as gradient similarity over (t,ϵ)(t,\boldsymbol{\epsilon}). In diffusion training, per-example losses and gradients depend on the noise level and Gaussian noise. Using notation from Sec. 2.1, define the per-example, per-draw diffusion gradient:

𝐠⁡(ϕ,𝐱,𝐜,t,ϵ)=∇ϕℓDiff​(Encode​(𝐱),𝐜,t,ϵ,ϕ)\mathbf{g}({\boldsymbol{\phi}};\mathbf{x},\mathbf{c},t,\boldsymbol{\epsilon})=\nabla_{{\boldsymbol{\phi}}}\ell_{\mathrm{Diff}}(\textnormal{Encode}(\mathbf{x}),\mathbf{c},t,\boldsymbol{\epsilon},{\boldsymbol{\phi}}) (58)

and let 𝒯\mathcal{T} denote a multiset of (t,ϵ)(t,\boldsymbol{\epsilon}) shared across query and training. A diffusion attribution score is the cosine similarity of normalized gradients, averaged over 𝒯\mathcal{T} [91]

Idiff​(n,query)=1|𝒯|​∑(t,ϵ)∈𝒯𝐠⁡(ϕ,𝐱query,𝐜query,t,ϵ)‖𝐠⁡(ϕ,𝐱query,𝐜query,t,ϵ)‖2⊤​𝐠⁡(ϕ,𝐱n,𝐜n,t,ϵ)‖𝐠⁡(ϕ,𝐱n,𝐜n,t,ϵ)‖2I_{\mathrm{diff}}(n,\mathrm{query})=\frac{1}{|\mathcal{T}|}\sum_{(t,\boldsymbol{\epsilon})\in\mathcal{T}}\frac{\mathbf{g}({\boldsymbol{\phi}};\mathbf{x}_{\mathrm{query}},\mathbf{c}_{\mathrm{query}},t,\boldsymbol{\epsilon})}{\|\mathbf{g}({\boldsymbol{\phi}};\mathbf{x}_{\mathrm{query}},\mathbf{c}_{\mathrm{query}},t,\boldsymbol{\epsilon})\|_{2}}^{\top}\frac{\mathbf{g}({\boldsymbol{\phi}};\mathbf{x}_{n},\mathbf{c}_{n},t,\boldsymbol{\epsilon})}{\|\mathbf{g}({\boldsymbol{\phi}};\mathbf{x}_{n},\mathbf{c}_{n},t,\boldsymbol{\epsilon})\|_{2}} (59)

where Idiff​(n,query)I_{\mathrm{diff}}(n,\mathrm{query}) abbreviates influence between (𝐱n,𝐜n)(\mathbf{x}_{n},\mathbf{c}_{n}) and (𝐱query,𝐜query)(\mathbf{x}_{\mathrm{query}},\mathbf{c}_{\mathrm{query}}). Sharing (t,ϵ)(t,\boldsymbol{\epsilon}) reduces ranking variance versus independent draws, while per-draw normalization mitigates scale effects. Estimating Eq. 59 is a Monte Carlo problem over (t,ϵ)(t,\boldsymbol{\epsilon}), and its variance affects influence ranking stability at fixed compute.

Why video is different: appearance-motion entanglement and length effects. For video, 𝐱∈ℝF×H×W×3\mathbf{x}\in\mathbb{R}^{F\times H\times W\times 3}, and the diffusion loss aggregates frame and spatial contributions. Two issues arise. First, whole-video gradients overemphasize static appearance (objects, backgrounds) over temporal dynamics. Second, gradient magnitudes scale with clip length FF, biasing similarity and selection toward longer clips.

Motion-centric attribution via loss-space masking (MOTIVE). MOTIVE [87] introduces a motion-weighted attribution loss that emphasizes dynamic regions (e.g., using optical-flow-derived motion magnitude) while suppressing static backgrounds, and corrects dominant length scaling. Let 𝐌⁡(𝐱)∈[0,1]F×H′×W′\mathbf{M}(\mathbf{x})\in[0,1]^{F\times H^{\prime}\times W^{\prime}} be a motion mask aligned with the latent grid (after any required downsampling), and let ℓ~Diff​(Encode​(𝐱),𝐜,t,ϵ,ϕ)∈ℝF×H′×W′\tilde{\ell}_{\mathrm{Diff}}(\textnormal{Encode}(\mathbf{x}),\mathbf{c},t,\boldsymbol{\epsilon},{\boldsymbol{\phi}})\in\mathbb{R}^{F\times H^{\prime}\times W^{\prime}} denote a per-location squared-error form of the diffusion cost. MOTIVE defines the motion-weighted per-example cost:

ℓmot​(ϕ,𝐱,𝐜,t,ϵ)=1F​meanf,h,w​[𝐌​(𝐱)f,h,w​ℓ~Diff​(Encode​(𝐱),𝐜,t,ϵ,ϕ)f,h,w]\ell_{\mathrm{mot}}({\boldsymbol{\phi}};\mathbf{x},\mathbf{c},t,\boldsymbol{\epsilon})=\frac{1}{F}\mathrm{mean}_{f,h,w}\big[\mathbf{M}(\mathbf{x})_{f,h,w}\tilde{\ell}_{\mathrm{Diff}}(\textnormal{Encode}(\mathbf{x}),\mathbf{c},t,\boldsymbol{\epsilon},{\boldsymbol{\phi}})_{f,h,w}\big] (60)

and the corresponding motion-weighted gradient:

𝐠mot​(ϕ,𝐱,𝐜,t,ϵ)=∇ϕℓmot​(ϕ,𝐱,𝐜,t,ϵ)\mathbf{g}_{\mathrm{mot}}({\boldsymbol{\phi}};\mathbf{x},\mathbf{c},t,\boldsymbol{\epsilon})=\nabla_{{\boldsymbol{\phi}}}\ell_{\mathrm{mot}}({\boldsymbol{\phi}};\mathbf{x},\mathbf{c},t,\boldsymbol{\epsilon}) (61)

which is substituted for 𝐠\mathbf{g} in Eq. 59. This isolates temporal dynamics while leaving the forward noising process unchanged, since the reweighting occurs only in the attribution loss.

Connection to variance reduction. Both IdiffI_{\mathrm{diff}} and its motion-weighted variant are Monte Carlo estimators over (t,ϵ)(t,\boldsymbol{\epsilon}) with expensive upstream encoding Encode​(𝐱)\textnormal{Encode}(\mathbf{x}), a natural target for the strategies in Sec. 3: timestep IS and stratification reduce variance over tt, and amortized re-noising reuses cached Encode​(𝐱)\textnormal{Encode}(\mathbf{x}) across (t,ϵ)(t,\boldsymbol{\epsilon}) draws.

Appendix C Additional Method Details

C.1 Variance Measurement Framework

Implementation details for the framework are summarized in Sec. 3.2.

C.1.1 Ground-Truth Estimation and Dispersion Metrics

For an unbiased estimator 𝝁^\hat{\boldsymbol{\mu}} of a target mean 𝝁\boldsymbol{\mu}, the variance Var⁡(𝝁^)=𝔼⁡[‖𝝁^−𝝁‖22]\mathrm{Var}(\hat{\boldsymbol{\mu}})=\mathbb{E}[\|\hat{\boldsymbol{\mu}}-\boldsymbol{\mu}\|_{2}^{2}] equals the mean squared error. We approximate 𝝁\boldsymbol{\mu} using a high-sample Monte Carlo reference 𝝁^GT\hat{\boldsymbol{\mu}}_{\mathrm{GT}} formed by averaging NGTN_{\mathrm{GT}} independent draws, typically NGT=1000​–​10,000N_{\mathrm{GT}}=1000\text{--}10{,}000 depending on the task. For a test estimator 𝝁^\hat{\boldsymbol{\mu}} with NN samples, we compute

Var^​(𝝁^)=‖𝝁^−𝝁^GT‖22\widehat{\mathrm{Var}}(\hat{\boldsymbol{\mu}})=\|\hat{\boldsymbol{\mu}}-\hat{\boldsymbol{\mu}}_{\mathrm{GT}}\|_{2}^{2} (62)

and average over multiple independent realizations (typically 50–200 trials) to reduce Monte Carlo noise in the variance estimate itself. This estimator inherits Var⁡(𝝁^GT)\mathrm{Var}(\hat{\boldsymbol{\mu}}_{\mathrm{GT}}) as additive bias; we draw 𝝁^GT\hat{\boldsymbol{\mu}}_{\mathrm{GT}} with the same variance-reduction strategy as each test estimator at NGT=20 000N_{\mathrm{GT}}{=}$20\,000$ samples (Sec. D.1.1, Sec. D.2.1), so the bias-to-test-variance ratio is ∼Ntest/NGT<1%{\sim}N_{\mathrm{test}}/N_{\mathrm{GT}}{<}\!1\% across all reported configurations, far smaller than the gaps between methods compared. We validate ground-truth quality by repeating the procedure with different random seeds and confirming agreement to within a small fraction of the standard error.

We measure variance at two stages of the SDS gradient pipeline:

  1. 1.

    Latent-space update (SDS residual): The vector 𝐟¯=1N​∑n=1NwSDS​(t(n))​𝐫(n)\bar{\mathbf{f}}=\frac{1}{N}\sum_{n=1}^{N}w_{\textnormal{SDS}}(t^{(n)})\mathbf{r}^{(n)} that multiplies the renderer Jacobian. This is the cheapest to compute because it does not require backpropagation through the renderer.

  2. 2.

    Parameter gradient: The full gradient ∇𝜽ℒSDS=1N​∑n=1N𝐟¯(n)​∂𝐱(n)∂𝜽\nabla_{{\boldsymbol{\theta}}}\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{SDS}}=\frac{1}{N}\sum_{n=1}^{N}\bar{\mathbf{f}}^{(n)}\frac{\partial\mathbf{x}^{(n)}}{\partial{\boldsymbol{\theta}}}, which includes the renderer Jacobian. This is more expensive but directly measures the quantity used for optimization.

Most prior work reports variance of the latent-space residual because it is easy to compute in a batched loop. However, the parameter gradient variance depends on the interaction between the residual and the renderer Jacobian, which can differ substantially across timesteps. We find that optimal importance-sampling proposals differ between the two metrics (see App. Fig. 23), so we report both and, when feasible, use parameter-gradient variance as our primary design criterion.

For parameter gradients, standard batched backpropagation aggregates contributions from all samples in a batch, so we cannot isolate individual sample gradients ∇𝜽ℒSDS(n)\nabla_{{\boldsymbol{\theta}}}\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{SDS}}^{(n)} without re-running backpropagation. To populate per-sample statistics, we use a batch size of 11 and loop over samples, which is expensive but necessary for accurate measurement. For DMD and data attribution, we follow a similar procedure, isolating per-sample contributions to the generator or denoiser gradients.

We also report cosine similarity between estimators and the ground truth,

CosineSim⁡(𝝁^,𝝁^GT)=𝝁^⊤​𝝁^GT‖𝝁^‖2​‖𝝁^GT‖2\mathrm{CosineSim}(\hat{\boldsymbol{\mu}},\hat{\boldsymbol{\mu}}_{\mathrm{GT}})=\frac{\hat{\boldsymbol{\mu}}^{\top}\hat{\boldsymbol{\mu}}_{\mathrm{GT}}}{\|\hat{\boldsymbol{\mu}}\|_{2}\|\hat{\boldsymbol{\mu}}_{\mathrm{GT}}\|_{2}} (63)

which captures directional alignment independent of magnitude. Unlike MSE, cosine similarity requires the ground truth to be precomputed and cannot be estimated online during training.

C.1.2 Cost Metrics and Extrapolation

We measure compute cost using three complementary metrics:

  • •

    Wall-clock time (ms): End-to-end time for a gradient step, including parallelization and GPU scheduling effects. This is the metric we use for effective compute multipliers in the main text.

  • •

    GPU memory (MB): Peak memory usage, which bounds feasible batch sizes and reveals parallelization headroom.

  • •
